   not the default workspace's records, change sets or publications. Changing the default
   workspace later does not change this workspace's selected release.
5. Check its **Overview**, model and applications. Use **Open workspace** to browse its data.
   Arrange data access separately; workspace creation does not grant every person access.
   To start an empty hierarchy, open its tree view and choose **Add …** for its top-level
   type. Create that record first, then add children beneath it; see
   [Arrange records in a tree](/docs/guide/use/arrange-records-in-a-tree/#add-the-first-top-level-record).

![New workspace dialog showing name, key and model choice](/docs/screens/workspaces-new-dialog.png)

**The workspace was not created** explains a refusal, such as a duplicate key or unusable release.
Correct that cause before retrying. **Cancel** leaves the list unchanged.
guide/src/content/docs/guide/model/make-:
---
title: Make a workspace the default
description: Select the default destination without changing other workspaces’ models or data.
reader: model-admin
---

You need **Workspace administration** and the deployment must allow workspace changes.
See [Managing workspaces](/docs/model/managing-workspaces/) for the default workspace's role.

1. Open **Settings › Workspaces**, then the active workspace you want as the default.
   Read its name, permanent key and model in **Overview**.
2. Choose **Set as default**. Check the success notice and **Default** mark afterwards.
   The previous default remains a separate workspace with its own records and model.
3. If another administrator changed the default while your page was open, read the notice,
   reload the state and choose again only if your intended change is still correct.
4. Inspect new-workspace creation choices when relevant: **The default workspace’s model**
   now refers to this workspace's release. Existing workspaces keep their selected releases.

![Workspace management showing the Default mark](/docs/screens/use-workspace-default.png)

Making a workspace default copies no records and grants no access. The default cannot be retired
or deleted. To take it out of use later, first select another active default.
guide/src/content/docs/guide/model/add-a:
---
title: Add a relationships table
description: Put both ends of a relationship and its own values in rows or a grid.
reader: model-admin
---

Add a relationships table when people need to maintain values belonging to connections between
records. Work in a draft with **Model authoring**. First [allow the relationship](/docs/guide/model/add-a-relationship/)
and choose what it carries. Read [columns and grouping](/docs/model/applications-and-views/#relationships-tables-columns-and-grouping)
for the model rules, and [Relationships tables](/docs/use/relationship-tables/) for the
result people use.

## Choose the relationship and columns

1. Select an application in the draft and choose **Add a view…**.
2. In **Kind of view**, choose **Relationships table: each relationship in a row, with its own attributes**. If it is absent, allow a relationship
   between two types first. Containment is not offered for this view.
3. In **Relationships**, choose the directed pair and relation. Read the arrow: the from end
   supplies grid rows, and the to end supplies column groups. The view reads this one pair,
   even when the relation type also connects other pairs.
4. In **Columns of the from record** and **Columns of the to record**, select and order the
   fields that identify each end. Keep at least one in each. Name and scalar fields are
   offered; fields holding JSON are not endpoint-column choices. The initial choice is Name
   and, where available, a unique scalar field. Changing Relationships resets these choices.
5. Under **Attributes of the relationship**, select the values to show. Only attributes carried
   by this pair are offered. An empty choice is allowed. Change the pair's **Carries** first if
   a needed value is missing. For a grid, choose the attributes people need under each column group.
6. Set **Layout** to **One row per relationship** or **Grid: each record once, a column group per
   related record**. Rows show existing connections. A grid also exposes gaps where people can
   link records. The first selected to-record field labels each grid column group.
7. For rows, **Head the rows by** chooses **Nothing: one list**, **The from record** or **The to
   record**. Group headings include counts. This choice does not group the grid.
8. Enter **Name** and choose **Add view**. Check the saved step, **Views** and **Issues**. The
   application lists either endpoint type if it was not already listed. No data is created.

![Add a relationships table with its directed pair, endpoint fields, relationship attributes and Layout choices](/docs/screens/model-add-relationships-table-layout.png)

*Above: Add a view to Network in a reference-model draft, with Stop to Operator through
Operated by, endpoint columns and the three relationship attributes. Layout is an open list
showing both choices, with Grid selected. Head the rows by and the name Stops of each operator
are also visible. This dialog has not been applied.*

## Understand the initial reading choices

The form derives filters from selected fields marked Filterable. It offers sorting by both
record names, selected endpoint fields and selected non-JSON relationship attributes, starting with the
from record's name. The reading size starts at 20. Filters, sort declarations and reading size
are not separate fields in this dialog. A specialist can adjust them in the
[JSON view](/docs/model/json-view/); the model checks their references and permits reading sizes
from 1 to 100.

In grid layout, people also get each endpoint type's main-view filters. They can narrow records
and choose displayed fields without changing the model. Their choices stay in that page's address.

## Change the layout and activate

1. In **Views**, open the relationships table's menu and choose **Layout…**.
2. Select either layout in the popover and choose **Save**. This changes the presentation of the same relationship;
   it does not duplicate or remove its connections.
3. Review **Issues**, then [install and activate the release](/docs/guide/model/install-and-activate-a-release/).
   Open the view in a workspace using the release and check its fields and available actions.

**Not applied** means the draft step was refused. Read the named issue and correct the pair or
field choices. **Cancel** leaves it unchanged. A publication is read-only, and live editing
still requires the person's data permissions; adding a view does not grant them.

**Remove relationships table** removes this presentation. Its confirmation also lists types
that stop being listed because only this view needed them. Review that list and any migration
warning before applying. The view does not own the stored relationships.
guide/src/content/docs/guide/model/retir:
---
title: Retire or delete a release
description: Stop offering a release for new use or remove an unused release with confirmation.
reader: model-admin
---

Open **Settings › Model**, then the model's **Releases** and the release. These lifecycle
changes need installation permission. See [Releases](/docs/model/releases/).

1. Check its version, workspace use and whether it runs the default workspace. **Retire…**
   stops new selection but keeps existing users on the release. The default workspace's release
   cannot be retired; move that workspace to another usable release first if appropriate.
2. Choose **Retire…**, read the named release and confirm. Cancel keeps it available. Check
   the **Retired** state afterwards. Workspaces and change sets already using it keep working.
3. To offer it again, choose **Bring back** and check that it is available. A model with every
   release retired and no running workspace appears under **Retired** in the model list.
4. Use **Delete…** only for a release with no remaining use or references. **Run by no workspace**
   alone does not prove it is deletable: records, publications, change sets, profiles or mappings
   can still refer to it. Read the confirmation and any refusal before proceeding.
5. Confirm deletion only when the named unused release is no longer needed. Deleting its release
   does not delete editable drafts. If refused, retain it or retire it; do not delete history to
   force a release removal.

![Release retirement confirmation](/docs/screens/release-retire-dialog.png)

If the release changed state elsewhere, reload it and review the current state before retrying.
Retirement is reversible; deletion is not the same operation.
guide/src/content/docs/guide/model/read-:
---
title: Read lists in a sheet
description: Check detected list ranges, exclude a list or choose how its cells become records.
reader: model-admin
---

Use this task when a sheet is laid out as several lists rather than one rectangular table.
Open its draft with **Model authoring**. See [Workbook onboarding](/docs/model/workbook-onboarding/).

1. Select the sheet in **Source**. For a sheet laid out as lists, select a detected list
   and read **Under**, **Cells**,
   **Note** and **Loads**. The cell preview shades the loaded range and shows a darker header;
   surrounding cells help you see whether its boundaries are right.
2. For a loaded list, choose **Adjust list…**. Set **Header row**, **Last row**, **First column**
   and **Last column**. Check the displayed range before applying. The cell outline is not
   a draggable range editor.
3. Choose **Don't load this list** to exclude it. A **Not loaded** notice explains why nothing
   reads a range: it may be empty, treated as free answers or interpreted another way.
4. For a range that really is a list, choose **Load as a list…** and review its interpretation.
   Check **Loads** again to see the type, key and any fixed parent it creates records under.
5. Where offered, review **Read these N lists as one list under their headers**. This proposal
   is for at least three same-shaped lists under one title or no title. It creates header records
   and values beneath them; a value beneath two headers becomes two records. Translated category
   names and the role of a second header row are not loaded by this choice.
6. Inspect **Issues** and each source's **Dry run** after changing a range or interpretation.
   **Note** identifies a skipped second header or explanatory row; check that it is not data
   you needed to keep. These edits never rewrite the uploaded spreadsheet's cells.

![Proposed list of fictional local stop codes, with its shaded range, reading instructions and adjustment actions](/docs/screens/model-workbook-list-range.png)

**Example.** The fictional local-code sheet above has its column headings on row 3,
but the proposal uses row 1 as the header. Review **Adjust list…** before loading it;
a detected range is a starting point, not confirmation that the headings are right.

If the cells cannot be read, use the displayed retry after correcting the cause. A reasonable
range alone does not establish that every resulting record passes the dry run.
guide/src/content/docs/model/model-mappi:
---
title: Model mappings
description: Map records between different workspace models, inspect losses and review the resulting change sets.
reader: model-admin
---

Use **Settings**, **Copy and move** when records need to go into a workspace whose model differs.
A model mapping says what each source type, field, parent and relationship becomes in the target.
It does not change either model. Follow
[Move records to another model](/docs/guide/model/move-records-to-another-model/).

This is different from a mapping grid: a grid relates records within a model; a model mapping
translates records between models. The source and target must be different workspaces.

## Proposals need your decision

Choose an existing mapping for the two models or ask for **A new mapping, proposed**. The engine
uses the models and shared record values to suggest matches. The editor shows source types on the
left, mapping choices in the centre and target types on the right. A saved mapping can be reused;
opening it does not copy records.

![Mapping editor with proposed type and field choices and a dry run summary](/docs/screens/model-mapping-proposed.png)

*Above: Guide mapping proposes Operators to Domains and Modes to Codelists between Graubünden and
Default. Those are suggestions to review, not a recommendation to use this mapping.*

**Proposed** means the choice is still the engine's suggestion. Select a row for **Why this step**
and read the supporting evidence. Alternatives offer other choices. A similarity
in fields or values does not prove the types mean the same thing.

![Selected mapping row with the proposal reason and alternative target types](/docs/screens/model-mapping-why.png)

*Above: Operator code is selected; alternatives change what Operator becomes in the target.*

![Proposal evidence expanded beside the selected mapping row](/docs/screens/model-mapping-evidence.png)

*Above: the evidence reports one of two fields shared, with values that convert. This observation
alone does not establish that an operator should become a domain.*

Edit a row's choice to make it yours. Review fields that are not carried, parent placement,
relationships and **Records already in the target**, not just the type names. Matching by a unique
field can find an existing target record; matching only records moved before is narrower. Records
found again are updated rather than duplicated. **Undo** and **Redo** revisit saved mapping steps.

## Choose records and inspect losses

**What to copy** or **What to move** offers every mapped type, the whole workspace, chosen types
with optional filters, or one record and everything under it. Unmapped types in a whole-workspace
selection are reported as left out. A subtree includes its contained descendants.

The dry run checks the selection without writing records. Review creates, updates, refused
records, carried relationships and dropped relationships. Open **What cannot be copied** or
**What cannot move** for each reason and its items. An unmapped field may lose its value even
when its record can be copied. A relationship can be carried only when its ends can be resolved
in the target; otherwise it is reported as dropped.

Correct a required value through a suitable mapping or default, place children under an allowed
parent, and map relationships you intend to keep. Do not add arbitrary defaults solely to make
a rejection disappear. A partial result needs a deliberate decision about what stays behind.
[Issues and dry runs](/docs/model/issues-and-dry-run/) explains the figures.

## Copy and move reach live data through review

**Copy** prepares a new change set in the target. Source records remain in place.
**Move** also prepares a deletion change set in the source. Review and publish the target copy
first, then review and publish the source deletions separately. The source deletion cannot be
published before its target copy. Records changed since the dry run, or needed by records staying
behind, are kept rather than silently deleted.

Starting the operation does not publish either change set. Review the actual job result as well
as the earlier prediction. A newer mapping version or changed model can invalidate confirmation;
refresh and review a new dry run before retrying. A selection with nothing eligible cannot start.

The **Mappings** list keeps reusable mappings. **Recent copies and moves** lists operations and
dry runs waiting to start; a dry run replaced by a later editor step is not listed.

## Access and availability

Copying and moving needs **Copy and move** access in the relevant workspaces. Reading records,
preparing change sets and publishing them require the corresponding workspace permissions too;
being a model author alone does not grant data publication rights. Ask an access administrator
when a step is refused. This flow also needs background jobs and model administration enabled
on the instance. When unavailable, the page explains why.

## Editor tabs and the running job

**Settings › Workspaces and models › Copy and move** lists saved Mappings with their source and target
models, version and updated time. **Recent copies and moves** lists workspace pairs, Copy or Move,
state, change sets and creation time. **Load more mappings** reads older mappings.

The editor uses **Mapping**, **Source**, **Target** and **Not copied** or **Not moved** tabs,
particularly on a phone. **Why this step** explains a proposed row with evidence and alternatives;
it shows no match score. If **The mapping names other releases than the workspaces run** appears,
choose **Use the releases the workspaces run**, inspect the affected rows and run the dry run
again before starting. Read **Copying and moving are read-only here** or **This editor reads
only** as a deployment restriction; ask the operator about model administration and jobs.

After starting, inspect the job's actual creates, updates, omissions and refusals and the links
to the produced change sets. Its result counts can differ from the dry run after intervening
changes. A completed job is not publication: review and publish the target proposal first and,
for a move, the source deletion proposal afterwards.

## Focused tasks and results

[Edit a mapping row](/docs/guide/model/edit-a-mapping-row/) covers targets, defaults and evidence.
[Choose what moves](/docs/guide/model/choose-what-moves/) covers selection and the loss report.

After completion, **Review the change set** opens the target changes and **Review the deletions**
opens the source deletion proposal for a move. Inspect deleted and kept counts and each reason.
**The copy did not complete** or **The move did not complete** means no publication happened;
inspect the job and any produced change sets before starting again. **Nothing to copy** or
**Nothing to move** needs a broader eligible mapping or selection, not repeated confirmation.
A running operation continues when you leave its page.

The job's result lists actual created, updated, refused or kept items and lost values or
relationships. **Items that cannot …** groups reasons; **No item has this reason any more**
means the current report no longer contains that group. **Values not carried** lists the type,
field, record count and reason. A report counts records, relationships and values separately.

Previously copied or moved records retain their correspondence between workspaces. Moving them
back can update their original counterparts rather than inventing duplicates; inspect the target
matching rule and dry run. This is different from splitting a model definition in a draft.
The browser mapping editor offers the rows described here; specialist mapping transformations
beyond those controls need an integrator. Release comparisons show relationships and views,
not changes to these separately saved model mappings.

## Delete a saved mapping

In **Mappings**, **Delete…** is shown to people with **Copy and move** access. The confirmation
is **Delete the mapping …?**. **Delete the mapping** removes the mapping together with its
history and proposals. **Cancel** keeps it. Copies and moves already made stay as they are;
a new operation needs another mapping. This is separate from deleting records or discarding
a change set. Deletion has no Undo in this list.

The delete uses the version you viewed. If someone changes the mapping first, deletion is
refused; refresh the list, inspect the new mapping and decide again. A failed deletion leaves
its error in the confirmation. Do not assume a mapping disappeared until the list removes it.
Follow [Delete a model mapping](/docs/guide/model/delete-a-model-mapping/) for the steps.
---
title: Migrations
description: Review conversions, renamed definitions and removals before switching a workspace’s model.
reader: model-admin
---

Use a migration when a workspace's records do not fit a selected model release unchanged.
The preview checks every record and lists conversions, type changes, created items, removals and
items that must be fixed. Workspace data stays unchanged until you confirm. You need **Model release** in the workspace;
background jobs and model administration must be available. Publication also needs the normal
data permissions and any required approval.

Start from the editor when a draft changes stored data, or from
[Change a workspace’s model](/docs/guide/model/change-a-workspaces-model/) for an installed release.
Follow [Migrate a workspace](/docs/guide/model/migrate-a-workspace/) to review and confirm.

## From an editor step to a migration

The editor applies changes to released elements, including key changes, moves, splits, merges,
removals and tighter rules. **History** marks steps that affect stored data **Needs a migration**;
a released key change needs one even with no records. Undo takes that step's part out of the
proposed migration; redo restores it. Saving a draft does not convert live data.

In **Install and activate…** or **Apply to this workspace…**, **Activation needs a migration**
states what the draft proposes. Review the steps, where records go, counts of records moving,
records and relationships created, and refused items. Each released key change warns that
integrations naming it must change and names the consumer APIs of the base release that use it.

**Install … and preview the migration…** installs the release and opens the migration page.
From Apply, use **Preview what happens to the records…**. The release is installed but the
workspace keeps its current release until you confirm the migration.

**What the draft proposes** opens filled in from the draft's remaining steps and the two models.
Its rows show **Records of**, **Become**, **In**, **Under** and **Records**, with a **Proposed** mark
for the draft's choice. Split, list-conversion and relationship-key changes appear beneath the rows.
Change **Become** to review another destination type, or **Not kept**; each choice previews again
without editing the draft. Check the new outcome before continuing.

![Migration preview with a Proposed destination row and outcome counts](/docs/screens/model-migration-proposed.png)

*Above: the draft proposes moving 12 Stop code records from Network to the top level of Systems. The row is marked Proposed, and Type changed counts 12 records; nothing has changed yet.*

## What the preview means

| Outcome | What to review |
| --- | --- |
| Converted | Values changed to the target definition's value type. Inspect before and after. |
| Type changed | Records kept under a new type, with their IDs and history. |
| Created | Records and relationships a split or list conversion creates. Shown when the migration creates them. |
| Removed | Records, values or relationships lost if you explicitly accept removal. |
| Must be fixed | Items blocking confirmation, such as missing required values or relationships, duplicate unique values or invalid parents. |

For each missing type or field, **Became …** says which target definition replaces it.
**Not kept** removes that type's records and relationships, or that field's values. Choices are
not merely labels: each starts a new preview. The page explains what is kept and what is removed.
Do not accept removal until you have inspected its individual items. While any item
**Must be fixed**, confirmation stays disabled and the loss-acceptance checkbox is hidden.
After those blockers are resolved, a preview with removals offers the acceptance checkbox.

![Migration review with missing-element choices and outcome counts](/docs/screens/model-migration-review.png)

The data conversion and workspace release switch succeed together. A failed execution does not
leave half a migration. A model release installed before this flow can remain installed even
when migration fails. Record history keeps what was removed; that is an audit trail, not an undo button.
Open change sets stay on their previous release until moved or discarded. Publications remain fixed.

## Cancellation, waiting and stale results

**Cancel the preview** stops a running preview; **Cancel** leaves a reviewed one unapplied.
The preview may briefly make writes to the live records it checks wait. Let it finish or cancel
before retrying a waiting edit. Leaving the page alone does not stop its background job.

Confirmation is bound to the reviewed workspace and data versions. After an intervening edit,
publication or model change, a stale-review notice asks for **Preview again**. Nothing was
migrated by the refused confirmation. Review every refreshed outcome before confirming again.
**Not migrated** and **Something went wrong** require reading the failure and correcting its
cause; they are not successful migration results.

## Change sets on another release

A change set can move to **the release its workspace currently runs**. **Move this change set
to …** opens the same review for its content. The page says nothing live changes. Confirmation
converts its content and updates its base and release together against current live records.
Conflicting authored records, relationships or mapping sets block the move. Open the resulting
change set, review it and validate before publishing normally.

Alternatively, **Move … to … and publish…** migrates the workspace to the change set's release
and publishes that change set in one step. The review explicitly says **Then publishes …** and
the confirmation says **Migrate and publish**. Required approval and publication conflicts still
apply; neither migration nor publication succeeds alone. Review the named publication afterwards.

Jobs retain the actual counts and item outcomes, with refused items prominent. Open only links
your permissions allow and compare the actual result with the preview. For moving data between
two workspaces instead, see [Model mappings](/docs/model/model-mappings/).

Value conversion uses supported source and target value-type pairs. A value that has no valid
conversion is listed as a loss; the preview does not invent a conversion for every pair of types.
Inspect those items before accepting removal. Activation can also suspend the selected workspace's
consumer subscriptions that its new contract no longer serves; other workspaces' subscriptions
are unaffected. Coordinate changed contracts with their owners before confirming.

## What the migration carries

- A renamed type or a merged type keeps its records under the resulting type. Renamed attributes
  carry their values to the new definitions. A relation type's new key carries its relationships.
- A type moved to another application takes its records to the application named by the draft,
  including when several applications list the type. A type the target release still has never
  loses its records: with no named application they go to the one application that lists the type,
  or the one that lists it newly; when several qualify the preview refuses them under **Must be
  fixed** and a mapping's application chooses. Moving from containment to the top level
  removes the old parent and its containment relationship. Under different parent types, records
  whose existing parent is no longer allowed appear under **Must be fixed**.
- A split creates a related record of the new type for each source record holding at least one
  moved value. It carries the selected values there. With **Many to one**, source records with
  identical moved values share one new record. The first moved value supplies its name, falling
  back to the source record's name. A source record holding none of those values gets no new record.
- A list conversion creates one list record per distinct value, named by that value, and connects
  each source record to its list record. The values leave the source records.
- Moving an attribute attachment to a different type removes its values from the original type's
  records. The preview lists this as loss: the destination type has different records, so moving
  the definition cannot transfer those values to them.
- Tighter requirements, number limits, value types and bounds are checked against stored data.
  Records breaking the target rules appear under **Must be fixed**; values that cannot convert
  appear as loss. Removing definitions also lists the lost content for explicit acceptance.

**Example:** a stop-code type that stood under stops in Network can move to the top level of
Systems. Its records keep their identities and values in Systems and lose their old stop parents.
This is one configuration of the same move available to any model.

To return to an earlier release, select that release and review its compatibility or migration.
This does not automatically recover content removed by an earlier migration.

## A move proposed by the assistant

A [model change from words](/docs/model/ai-model-changes/) can prepare whole-type mappings
for this preview. You still inspect and confirm the migration yourself; no change set is
created for a whole-type move. For an AI-written account, ask in the activation or Apply
dialog before coming here: [Explain a model change](/docs/guide/model/explain-a-model-change/).
The migration page itself lists conversions, removals and refusals without an AI account.
guide/src/content/docs/model/releases.md:
---
title: Releases
description: Understand immutable model releases, workspace activation and compatibility checks.
reader: model-admin
---

Install a draft to keep a fixed model release. Activate that release to make one workspace use
its definitions. These stages are separate even when the editor offers them in one confirmation.
Follow [Install and activate a release](/docs/guide/model/install-and-activate-a-release/).

## An installed release never changes

A release records its model name, stable release key, version and schema. The version distinguishes
releases of your model; the schema identifies the model language. Neither is a draft's edit count.
To change definitions, make a draft and install another release. You cannot overwrite a release's
content by reusing its identity for different definitions.

Open **Settings**, **Model**, choose a model and select **Releases**. The list shows its installed
versions, schema, installation date and workspace use. **Drafts** lists editable work separately,
with each draft's base release.

![Installed versions on a model's Releases tab](/docs/screens/model-releases.png)

*Above: the Graubünden model has one installed release, 1.0.0, used by Graubünden.*

![Drafts listed separately with their base release and date](/docs/screens/model-drafts.png)

*Above: Guide draft and another draft both start from the Graubünden model's release 1.0.0.*

Open a release to inspect its counts and workspace use, **Create draft from release**, or
**Activate in a workspace…**. **Structure** on the model’s page is read-only and initially selects the newest release;
its Release picker can show another version.

![Read-only model structure with application and type counts](/docs/screens/model-structure.png)

*Above: the newest Graubünden release lists Network's types and the other applications.*

The release's **Changes in this release** section lets you choose **Compare with**. It shows
added, changed and removed definitions relative to that choice. Check the before and after
release names: a chosen comparison may be another model rather than this release's predecessor.
With no earlier release, there may be nothing to compare until you choose a baseline.

## Activation belongs to one workspace

Each workspace runs its own release. Different workspaces may run different versions or entirely
different models. Making a release available does not switch every workspace. The default workspace
is simply the default destination; it does not impose its model on the rest.

![Workspace overview identifying its model and applications](/docs/screens/model-workspace-model.png)

*Above: Graubünden runs Public transport stops of Graubünden 1.0.0 and offers Edit model.*

![A second workspace overview with a different model and applications](/docs/screens/model-workspace-other-model.png)

*Above: Default runs RDM Starter Model 0.10.0 alongside Graubünden, with its own applications.*

Activation checks the target workspace's records, values and relationships. It is refused when
those data do not fit unchanged, or when consumer API compatibility requires another contract
version. A release that fitted yesterday can fail today if data changed. Selecting an older release
is subject to the same checks; it is not a way to undo record edits.

When you open **Edit model** from a workspace, the editor identifies it with **Applies to** and
**Apply to this workspace…**. The confirmation lists the model differences, data compatibility,
consumer API compatibility, other workspaces left unchanged and open change sets left behind.
If data needs migration, it offers **Preview what happens to the records…** for a separate review
and confirmation. Opening that preview alone changes nothing.

## Change sets keep their release

Activating a new release does not rewrite open change sets. They remain pinned to their old
release and cannot be published while the workspace runs a different one. The confirmation lists
them so you can plan the change. Move each to the new release and validate it, or discard it
through the change-set workflow. Publications remain fixed snapshots.

See [Change sets](/docs/use/change-sets/) before applying a model change beside work in progress.

## Retiring a release

A release can be **Retired** to stop it being chosen for new work. Workspaces and change sets
already on it keep working. On the release page, **Retire…** asks for confirmation; **Bring back**
makes a retired release available again. The default workspace's release cannot be retired.
These controls need installation permission.

Deletion is more restrictive: a release must have no remaining references. A running workspace,
history, an import profile or a mapping can prevent deletion, and the refusal explains why.
Deleting a release does not delete its drafts. Read the confirmation before using **Delete release**.

## Read the result of both stages

**Installed, not active** means installation succeeded but the workspace did not switch. The
installed release remains available. Resolve the reported reason and activate that release from
its page; do not assume a second installation is needed. A concurrency refusal means the workspace
or draft changed after your check: refresh, review the current state and check again.

If the mutation controls are unavailable, check your permissions in
[Models](/docs/model/models/#who-may-do-what) and whether model administration is enabled.

## Availability, details and checks

The page marks **Runs this release** for a workspace using it and **Run by no workspace** when
none does. Under **Technical details**, **Release ID** and **Content hash** each have **Copy**;
these identify a release and its exact content, rather than its displayed version alone.
**Export JSON** downloads the immutable model document for a specialist model author.

**Activation check** checks each workspace running this model separately. Read the workspace name
and result; a successful check for one workspace says nothing about another's data. A failed
check is not compatibility. The confirmation checks again when you activate.

**Retire…** removes a release from new choices without changing workspaces already running it.
**Bring back** makes it available again. A release never run and with no records, change sets or
publications made under it can offer **Delete…** with confirmation. Retirement preserves the
release; deletion removes an unused one. A model with all releases retired and no running
workspace appears under Retired.

Release pickers offer usable releases supported by this refiroo version. A new workspace starts
with the newest release of each model offered, with older versions available on request.
A change set offers every usable version and its own workspace's release even if that release
is retired. Older unsupported releases remain inspectable and exportable; ask the operator
about updating their model-language version before using them again.

## Tasks and checks

[Compare releases](/docs/guide/model/compare-releases/),
[Retire or delete a release](/docs/guide/model/retire-or-delete-a-release/) and
[Export a release](/docs/guide/model/export-a-release/) cover the release page's actions.
[Change a workspace's model](/docs/guide/model/change-a-workspaces-model/) explains the activation
results; [Migrations](/docs/model/migrations/) explains conversion and explicit acceptance of loss.
[Model language versions](/docs/model/model-language-versions/) explains a historical release that
cannot be used by this deployment.

The release page's **Activation check** covers workspaces running this model. A workspace running
another model is checked separately when selected as a destination. **Historical release** means
this deployment cannot interpret its model language for the usual comparison and activation checks;
its metadata and raw export remain readable.

Installation makes the installed release the draft's base without resetting its editing
version. A second different definition under the same release key and version is refused; the
install dialog proposes an editable next version. Exact reinstallation of the same content can
restore a retired release. After a switch, an older open data form may be refused because it
was based on the old model; reload and review the new definitions before editing again.

Open change sets can use **Change model version** only when their content already fits the
chosen release. If conversion is needed, use the migration review. Starting a change set from
current live data likewise checks that its selected model can hold that data; choosing a model
version does not waive its rules. Publication requires a successful validation of the current
change-set version and agreement with the workspace's active release. See
[Change sets](/docs/use/change-sets/) for the ordinary creation and publication steps.

## Ask what activation changes

With a configured AI provider and the required workspace permissions, the activation dialog
offers **What this change does**. [Accounts of model changes](/docs/model/model-change-accounts/)
explains the facts, sent data, costs and limits. Follow
[Explain a model change](/docs/guide/model/explain-a-model-change/) to ask; opening the dialog
alone makes no provider request.

guide/src/content/docs/model/ai-model-ch:
---
title: Model changes with the assistant
description: Review a model proposed from words or a workbook, and understand how its records move.
reader: model-admin
---

Describe the model you need in words and the assistant proposes a draft for you to review.
You can attach a workbook, but a file is not required. The assistant can add fields, types,
relationships and applications, or propose moving records between types. These are model
capabilities available to any application.

Start with [Change a model with the assistant](/docs/guide/model/change-a-model-with-the-assistant/).
For a file that needs a model and a load, follow
[Review the assistant's workbook design](/docs/guide/model/review-an-assistants-workbook-design/).
The [model editor](/docs/model/the-model-editor/) remains available for direct edits.

## Availability and your data

The built-in assistant uses Claude Code. It is available only when your operator has enabled it
and allows the data it needs to be sent. Your words and the workspace's model go to Claude Code,
with the whole workbook if attached. The assistant reads workspace records as needed, within
your permissions. This is more than sending a few sample rows.

**Change this model…** is offered in an active workspace when you hold **Use AI proposals**,
**Bulk and import**, **Work in change sets**, **Model authoring** and **Model release**, and job
creation is enabled. Installing a changed model also needs **Model release** at instance level.
If the offer is missing, ask your administrator to check these rights and the assistant setup.
The separate AI provider used for explanations does not enable this assistant.

Assistant turns can incur Claude Code usage charges. refiroo records who asked, the outcome,
tokens and cost when reported. Tasks and workbooks normally remain for 90 days after completion
or the last change. Session files and transcripts remain while the task can continue; cleanup
follows publication, discard, confirmed migration or expiry. These are separate from optional
logging of request content. See [About AI in refiroo](/docs/run/ai/) for the full explanation of
access, billing, data leaving the instance and retention, including the provider's own policies.

## Review the proposal before accepting

**The assistant’s proposal** describes the types it would add or change and any records it
would move. Read the counts and **Checks**, not only the summary. The assistant's wording can
be wrong. The engine checks the draft and the data against its rules; that does not establish
that the proposed design means what you intended.

Answer the questions or use **Tell the assistant what to change**. You can also choose
**Open in the model editor** and edit the draft directly. The same assistant reads those edits
when it continues. A second assistant task cannot take over a draft another task holds.

For a workbook load, **What the load does** shows new and matched records, new relationships,
refused items and rows read. Open a type's row for example records with their source cells,
read any **One name twice in one type** finding, and expand **Where each part of the file goes**
to review how the file is used. The assistant reads the file, model and workspace records and
prepares records and relationships for the engine to check; it writes no import profile.

**Accept and load to change set** lets the engine install the changed model and load exactly those checked
records and relationships into a new change set as one batch. No assistant turn runs, and nothing
is activated or published. A draft changed after the check is checked again first; any refusal
then prevents installation and loading. If changed data causes a refusal during the batch, none
of the batch is loaded and the change set is discarded. A release installed before that failure
can remain installed. Correct the proposal in words, review the new check and accept again.
An assistant load saves no profile for the next file; send that file to the assistant again.

Model-only and record-move proposals keep **Accept the model**. A whole-type move still needs
migration confirmation. A partial move still needs publication. Loading an already saved layout
is a separate path: its confirmation can install and activate a model change before importing.
Read the confirmation for the path you are using.

## Only the model changes

When the request changes the model alone, such as adding a view without changing records,
acceptance installs the release and ends with a migration that moves no type. Review
**Preview the migration** and confirm it with **Model release** to put the workspace on the
new model. No change set is created and every record stays as it is.

## Every record of a type moves

A whole type becoming another type, two types merging, or a type moving into another application
can use a migration. The proposal lists what each type becomes and how many records it holds.
Accepting installs the proposed release but moves no record. **Preview the migration** opens
the existing migration review with the proposed choices filled in.

Someone with **Model release** confirms that migration. It changes live data and the workspace's
release together, keeping record IDs, values, relationships and history for the accepted type
moves. There is no change set to submit for approval in this path. Inspect every conversion,
removal and refusal in the [migration preview](/docs/guide/model/migrate-a-workspace/).

## Only some records move

For a split based on a field value, the proposal describes what acceptance prepares: a
release holding the old types beside the new ones, a change set moving the selected records,
and the final release removing the emptied types. The removal note says which records move
and where they go. After accepting, complete the prepared steps:

1. Activate the release holding the new types beside the old. No record moves yet.
2. Review and publish the change set, following the workspace's approval rules. The records
   change type and keep their IDs.
3. Activate the final release, removing the emptied types. If someone has added records to an
   old type meanwhile, activation is refused until that is resolved.

The task shows the next available step and marks completed steps **Done**. If the old types
remain in the accepted model, it shows **Two steps are yours** instead: no final removal is needed.
A whole-type move and a partial move need separate tasks. Splitting thousands of top-level
records can be slow because those records are prepared one at a time.

## Stop, correct or discard

**Stop** ends the current turn. A stopped correction returns to the last proposal, with a
warning if it already changed the draft. A stopped load discards the change set it was making
and returns to the accepted proposal. Before any proposal exists, the stopped task still takes
words telling the assistant how to continue.

A failed task shows its reason. Use **Tell the assistant how to go on**, or **Try again as it was**.
A stopped task offers **Go on as it was**. **Discard this task** ends it and removes its draft;
if it has a loaded change set, that is discarded too. Discard does not reverse a confirmed
migration or an already published change.

For a loaded change set that is wrong, **Discard and load again** removes that change set,
including your manual edits in it. For a workbook load, the assistant then revises the proposal
and checks its records again. Review it and choose **Accept and load to change set** to prepare the replacement
change set. Review the discard confirmation carefully. Once published, the task offers new work through **Change this model…** or
**Ask about these records…**, subject to your current permissions.
guide/src/content/docs/model/issues-and-:
---
title: Issues and dry runs
description: Distinguish model validity, compatibility with stored records and predicted data changes.
reader: model-admin
---

Check a model before applying it. refiroo answers three different questions: are the definitions
valid, does the selected workspace's data fit, and what happens to incoming or moved records?
A green result for one question does not answer the others.

## Issues in a draft

Expand **Issues and history**, then choose **Issues**. Each issue gives its severity, message and,
where available, a link to the affected element. The header also reports the validation state.
A draft can be saved while invalid so you can repair it in several steps. It cannot be installed
until its blocking model errors are resolved.

![Issues tab naming an unavailable field and linking to its view](/docs/screens/model-issues-error.png)

*Above: a deliberate error in Guide draft makes the Municipalities view refer to a field that
is not available. The issue links to the view, and the header says 1 error.*

Read the whole message. A missing field in a view may need removing from the view, or attaching
the intended field to its record type. Creating another field simply to silence the message can
leave the wrong design in place. Recheck after the correction.

**No issues** means the draft is valid. With a workbook, the list also includes import-profile
warnings and errors. Warnings need review even when they do not block model installation; a
valid model can still have refused source rows.

![Issues tab showing no issues and a Valid header](/docs/screens/model-issues-none.png)

*Above: Guide draft is valid again after the faulty view setting was corrected.*

Follow [Fix issues before installing](/docs/guide/model/fix-issues-before-installing/).

## Does stored data fit?

**Install and activate…**, **Apply to this workspace…** and an installed release's
**Activate in a workspace…** check the selected workspace's data. Compatibility means its records,
values and relationships fit without migration. It does not copy data from another workspace.

A removed type still holding records, a newly required field with missing values, duplicate values
under a uniqueness rule, or too many relationships under a tighter cardinality can prevent a
switch. Read the named data and reason. Correct the data under the current model, revise the draft,
or use the offered migration preview where records must move. Ordinary activation does not silently
convert or discard incompatible records.

Consumer APIs are checked separately. A change that breaks what other systems read needs a higher
contract version before activation. Review the listed differences with the people responsible for
those systems before using **Raise to v…**. This is separate from the model release version.

A check reflects the data and versions it read. Another edit or activation can invalidate it;
refiroo checks again at the write boundary and can refuse the confirmation.

## A workbook's dry run

With an attached workbook, **Dry run** checks the whole mapped file against the draft and the
comparison workspace without writing records. It identifies the draft version and check time.
Figures include records created or updated, values, relationships, related records created and
refused rows. Open a figure to inspect the rows and reasons behind it. A **was** figure compares
with the previous result.

Wait for **Checked** after an edit. **Checked** means the file was checked, not that every row
was accepted. **Failed** or **Stopped** is not a completed result. Read the failure and retry;
do not rely on a result from an older draft version. A draft without a workbook has no file rows
to check. See [Workbook onboarding](/docs/model/workbook-onboarding/) for this flow and its screenshots.

## A copy or move dry run

Between workspaces with different models, a dry run checks every selected item through a mapping.
Its five summary figures count different things:

| Figure | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Create | Records to add in the target. |
| Update (copied before or found) | Target records found again and updated instead of duplicated. |
| Cannot be copied / Cannot move | Records refused or left out. |
| Relationships carried | Relationships that can be represented in the target. |
| Relationships dropped | Relationships refused or left out by the mapping or selection. |

**What cannot be copied** or **What cannot move** groups the reasons and lists affected items.
A **Value not carried** can leave a record copied without that field; a refused record is left out
entirely. Do not read an item total as a count of records: the report also concerns relationships
and values.

![Copy dry run report grouping refused records, dropped relationships and values not carried](/docs/screens/model-mapping-dry-run.png)

*Above: the Graubünden-to-Default dry run predicts 79 records created. Its report includes invalid
parents, missing required values and unmapped relationships. Nothing has been copied.*

Use **Open the mapping** on an item to repair the relevant choice. Review a fresh dry run after
changing the mapping or selection. See [Model mappings](/docs/model/model-mappings/) for the rules
and [Move records to another model](/docs/guide/model/move-records-to-another-model/) for the task.

Some issues offer a direct fix, such as **Use as the profile's key** or removing a panel naming
a removed field. Read what the action changes before choosing it, then recheck the issues.
A workbook's Dry run has separate source tabs; inspect each, including the dialog listing
refused sheet rows for its type. The figures' **was** values compare with the last check, not
with a completed import.
guide/src/content/docs/model/types-attri:
---
title: Types, attributes and relations
description: Define kinds of record, shared fields, allowed connections and containment.
reader: model-admin
---

Define a type for each kind of record people maintain. Its attributes hold values; its
relationships connect records. You need **Model authoring** to change these definitions in a draft.
[Models](/docs/model/models/) explains when changes reach a workspace.

## Types and where records stand

The editor calls a record type an **Object type**. **Name** is singular; **Plural name** labels
its collection. **Stands** places it at the top level or under another type. A child is joined
to its parent by a containment relation, with names in both directions. Containment is not an
extra label on an ordinary relationship: it defines the record hierarchy too.

A type may be listed in several applications while keeping one definition and one set of rules.
Removing a listing differs from removing the type. Follow
[Add a record type and fields](/docs/guide/model/add-a-record-type-and-fields/) or
[Split, merge and move types](/docs/guide/model/split-merge-and-move-types/).

## Attributes and shared definitions

An attribute type defines a reusable field, including its name, value type and features.
The value types offered are **Text**, **Long text**, **Whole number**, **Decimal number**, **Yes or no**, **Date**,
**Date and time** and **JSON**.
Choose the type for the value people hold, rather than storing every value as text.

An attachment to a record type determines **Required** and **Read-only** there. **Unique** belongs
to the shared attribute definition. Changing a shared name, value type or feature affects every
attached type; **Shared with** identifies them. A required field needs a value; a read-only field
cannot be changed through the ordinary record form. **Searchable** includes the field in search and **Filterable** permits filtering. Views choose
which filter controls they offer. **Sortable** is shown, but ordinary non-JSON fields can sort
from list headers regardless of that checkbox. These features do not select table columns.
JSON fields cannot be made unique, sorted or filtered. They can be displayed in a table or
record field; they are not eligible as candidate criteria or scalar labels for trees and matrix
column headings.

![Released Stop type with its attribute rules and key-change migration notice](/docs/screens/model-type-fields.png)

*Above: Stop has nine attributes with their value types and local rules. Its facts say Released: a key change needs a migration.*

[Reuse and change attributes](/docs/guide/model/reuse-and-change-attributes/) explains the controls.
The visual editor sets numeric bounds and effective periods. Attribute defaults need a specialist in the [JSON view](/docs/model/json-view/).
The editor does not offer text-format or length rules.
A list of reference choices is modelled as related records, rather than as another value type:
[Turn an attribute into a list](/docs/guide/model/turn-an-attribute-into-a-list/).

## Relationships and permitted pairs

A relation type supplies the forward and reverse meanings. Permitted pairs separately say which
types it may join. Their **Cardinality** limits the number of connections at each end;
**Required** declares dependent ownership: the target is created with its owner connection.
It is supported for one-to-one or one-to-many relationships; **Many to one** cannot be required. **Which records** can narrow candidates by name,
attached attributes or ancestor. Criteria can apply to the records chosen and the records choosing.
Do not confuse a candidate rule with a filter that hides rows in one view.

**Relationship matrix** shows all permitted type pairs. Rows are the from end. Each cell lists
the relation types and number limits, with **contains** for containment. Select a pair to inspect
or change its permissions. This design grid differs from a relation matrix that people use for data.

![Relationship matrix with a selected from and to pair](/docs/screens/model-matrix-pair.png)

Follow [Add a relationship](/docs/guide/model/add-a-relationship/).

The attributes carried by a permitted pair belong to each connection, not to either record.
**Reference-data example:** Operated by, from Stop to Operator, carries Local name (Text),
Primary contact (Yes or no) and Inspected on (Date). Maps to, from System code to Municipality,
carries Confirmed (Yes or no) and Note (Text). These fields describe each connection, so
connections to the same operator or municipality can hold different values. The model chooses
which fields each permitted pair carries.

Choose the shared definitions in the pair's **Carries** cell. All eight attribute value types
listed above are available. The pair is directed: the selected from type, relation and to type
determine which attributes it carries. Opening the same connection from its other end reads
the same stored values; it does not create a second set. Another permitted pair using the same
relation type can carry different attributes.

People see these values in the record's Relationships panel and a relation matrix's cell table.
A [relationships table](/docs/use/relationship-tables/) can put them beside both records or
under column groups in a grid. Follow [Add a relationships table](/docs/guide/model/add-a-relationships-table/)
to choose its layout. Declaring carried attributes does not add a view by itself.
A [consumer API](/docs/model/consumer-apis/) can explicitly expose these values within a related
block; carrying a field does not automatically publish it to other systems.

## Released elements and migrations

You can rename, re-key, remove or reshape a released element in the editor. Labels change
without changing identity. A released key can also change, but needs a migration even when
there are no records: integrations naming the old key must change with it.

A structural step that affects stored data applies to the draft and is marked **Needs a migration**
in **History**, with the records, values and relationships that hold the element. The counts cover
Live and open change sets in every workspace running the draft’s model; workspaces running
other models and immutable publications are not counted. A structural step with nothing holding
the element has no mark, except for a released key change. Activation checks the data again.

Menus warn **Needs a migration when installed**. Saving the step does not change live data.
Installing the draft shows the migration to review before activating it. See
[Migrations](/docs/model/migrations/) for what is carried, created, removed or refused.

See [Rename or re-key an element](/docs/guide/model/rename-or-re-key-an-element/) and
[Remove an element](/docs/guide/model/remove-an-element/).

## Rules beyond the visual forms

The type’s **Settings** chooses a **Display attribute**, an **Effective period**, **At least one of**
and **Parent relationships**. A display
field must be attached to its type. An effective period uses appropriately typed fields and
requires a valid date order. Relationship attributes retain their types just as record fields do.

A relationship’s uniqueness rule can also be limited by a declared ancestor scope or condition. Those references
must resolve to the appropriate type and field. Such rules apply to writes through all clients;
a hidden field or filtered view does not bypass them. The visual candidate editor offers
**Which records may be chosen** and **Which records may choose**, with names, fields and ancestor
fields. Candidate criteria govern new choices; a later value change does not automatically remove
an existing relationship.

A mapping grid's relation cannot be containment or required ownership. Resolve the named model
issue by selecting a suitable relationship, rather than treating an application name as a special
permission to use the view. For the visual relation controls, select a **Relation type** to edit
**Names** and **Reverse name** and inspect **Allowed between**. **Allow between two types…**
chooses the From and To pair; **Change keys…** changes the identifying keys. Released key changes
need a migration, and integrations naming those keys must change too.

## Lists are types too

Give each independently maintained list its own record type. Its relationships then offer the
right kind of record without filtering by a parent's spelling. A list can have its own fields,
related names and external codes. Do not tie a model definition to one existing record as a way
to select a list: record values change independently of model releases. Use separate types and
[group their collections](/docs/guide/model/group-collections-in-navigation/) when there are many.

## Value rules

A declared default supplies a missing field on creation. It does not refill a cleared value on
an existing record. Required fields cannot be empty; empty text counts as missing. For an ordinary
unique field, a non-empty value can be held by only one record in the workspace, across all types
that use that shared definition. Empty values do not reserve a value. A change set checks its own
effective data, and publication checks again against changes made elsewhere.

Whole-number and decimal fields may have a minimum, a maximum or both. Bounds must be finite
numbers, and the minimum cannot exceed the maximum. The same bounds apply wherever the shared
field is used, including declared relationship fields. A value outside a bound is refused; change
the value or review the intended definition. Other value types cannot declare numeric bounds.

A type can also require at least one of a declared group of fields. This differs from making
each field required. The rule checks the complete result of an edit, including clearing a field:
people cannot clear the last populated field in that group. All named fields must be attached
to the type. Choose **At least one of…** in the type’s Settings to select the group. Clear every selection
to remove the grouped requirement. Set numeric bounds through an attribute type’s
**Minimum and maximum…**; leave either end empty for no bound. Attribute defaults still need
a specialist in the JSON view.

## Number limits and ownership

| Cardinality | Limit at each end |
| --- | --- |
| One to one | A source has at most one target and a target at most one source. |
| One to many | A source may have many targets; each target has at most one source. |
| Many to one | A source has at most one target; a target may serve many sources. |
| Many to many | Neither end is limited to one by this rule. |

These limits are counted for the relation type at the limited end, including its other allowed
type pairs. Adding another permitted pair does not give a record another single-choice slot.

For required one-to-one or one-to-many ownership, the source owns the dependent target. The target
is created with that relationship; people cannot remove the connection alone and leave an invalid
dependent. Confirmed cascade deletion of the owner also deletes its dependants. For an optional
association, removing the source's connections preserves the independent records at the other end.
Containment cascade deletes descendants. In a change set these deletions remain proposed until
publication; an existing publication stays unchanged.

A relationship stores only the fields declared for its allowed type pair. With no declared
relationship fields, it cannot hold arbitrary extra values. Supplied values keep the shared
field's type and numeric bounds. Relationship fields are separate from either endpoint's fields.

A type may contain more records of its own type, allowing several levels without creating a
new type for each level. Declaring that structure does not itself add a tree view: choose its
presentation separately. Move a record through its parent controls; a containment connection
cannot be edited independently of the parent. refiroo keeps the parent and its typed connection
together when records are created or moved.

A specialist can limit a relationship to one target per source and named ancestor of the target.
For example, a record may have one current related name under each language record. A condition
on a target field can restrict which relationships reserve that slot. The rule checks live data
and a change set's effective data, then checks the merged result at publication. Older publications
do not reserve slots in current data. This is a relationship uniqueness rule, separate from a
field's workspace-wide uniqueness.

A relation's discovery hint does not expand ordinary record search through its connections.
Search uses record names and searchable fields. Creation controls and hierarchy presentation
come from the declared panels and views, rather than from a relation's descriptive hints alone.

## Candidate criteria

The two ends can have different criteria. With none, any record of the allowed type is eligible.
Criteria can name the record's name, any attached non-JSON field, or a name or field of an ancestor.
The field need not be filterable in collection views.

| Field | Conditions offered |
| --- | --- |
| Text or long text | **is**, **contains**, **starts with**; the last two ignore case. |
| Numbers, dates and times | **is**, **is less than**, **is at most**, **is more than**, **is at least**. |
| Yes or no | **is**, with yes or no. |
| Any offered field | **is empty**, with yes or no. |
| Attached attribute | Also **has no value**, with yes or no, to test whether a value is held at all. |

Criteria use “and”, except that several **is** values on one field are alternatives. When
several criteria name one ancestor type, one ancestor must satisfy them together. In a recursive
hierarchy any ancestor of that type can qualify, at any depth. Unknown fields, an impossible
ancestor type, JSON fields, unsuitable conditions and wrongly typed values prevent a valid model.

The same eligibility governs relationship pickers, bulk relationship changes, mapping grids
and relation matrices. It also governs loads and writes from other clients. A grid normally
omits an ineligible source, but keeps it visible when it already has the relationship. Removal
still lists existing connections.

Changing values or criteria never automatically removes an existing connection, flags it as
invalid or blocks publication just because it no longer qualifies. The rules apply to new choices.
Use a purpose-made Yes/No field where possible: a condition on a name follows that name when
someone renames the record. Follow [Add a relationship](/docs/guide/model/add-a-relationship/)
to edit **Which records may be chosen** and **Which records may choose**.

## Effective periods

A type can declare one period of business validity using two different attached **Date** fields.
**Date and time** fields cannot define this period. The starting date is included; the ending date
is excluded. An empty start means no beginning limit; an empty end means no ending limit. Different
records' periods may overlap.

When both dates are present, the end must be later than the start. Equal dates are invalid.
The rule applies to live edits, change-set edits, validation and publication. Activating a release
that adds a period or changes its fields also checks existing records and refuses invalid periods.
Correct the affected dates under the current model or revise the declaration before retrying.

This period is independent of record versions, history and publications. Other systems can read
records valid on a chosen business date when the type declares a period. Removing the declaration
keeps the date values but removes that date-based reading capability; for an exposed type this
can require a higher consumer contract version. To set the period, open the type’s **Settings**, edit **Effective period**, and choose
**Starts on** and **Ends on**. The control is offered when two Date attributes are attached,
or a period already exists. Choose **None: records have no effective period** in Starts on
to remove it. Check existing dates before applying the release.

## Visibility, help and relationship settings

A type’s **Attributes** table has editable **Hidden** and **Help text** cells. Hidden leaves a
field off record screens and forms; it does not remove its values or its validation rules.
Do not hide a required field unless records can obtain its value another way. At **Attribute
types**, the shared definition’s **Settings** applies Hidden and Help text wherever it is used.
A locally hidden field stays hidden; a local No does not reveal a field hidden by its shared
definition. Local help text takes precedence over shared help text; clearing it uses the shared text.
Neither setting grants or removes access to stored data.

Select a **Relation type** and edit **Oriented** in **Settings**. It defaults to Yes.
This affects cascade deletion: an oriented required one-to-one or one-to-many relationship
can take the owned target records with its source. Optional relationships lose the connection
while keeping the other record. Containment descendants are included independently.
It does not rename the two directions or change their number limits.

On a type’s **Relations** table, **Carries** shows the shared attributes attached to that
allowed pair. Choose **Attributes of the relationship…** to select them. This is available
for non-containment pairs with attribute definitions to choose from; changing a released pair
that stored data uses can need a migration. **Cardinality and required…** edits the pair’s number and ownership
rules together. Saving definitions creates no relationships or values between actual records.

**Parent relationships…** selects incoming relationships that supply parent context for this
type in trees and matrices. It is a draft-only structural choice. It differs from moving an
existing record or choosing its containment parent. Review the eligible choices and Issues;
do not use it to bypass the type’s placement rules.
