guide/src/content/docs/model/models.md:
---
title: Models
description: Shape applications, record types, fields, relationships and views through drafts and releases.
reader: model-admin
---

Use a model to decide what people can keep in a workspace and how they work with it.
A model defines applications, record types, fields, relationships, hierarchies and views.
Changing a model changes those definitions; editing a record changes the data held under them.
Start with [Create a model draft](/docs/guide/model/create-a-model-draft/).

## What a model contains

| Part | What it decides |
| --- | --- |
| Applications | Named work areas and the types and views available in each. |
| Object types | The kinds of record people can create. The editor calls a record type an **Object type**. |
| Attribute types | Reusable field definitions, such as a date or a whole number. A type attaches an attribute and decides whether it is required or read-only there. |
| Relation types | The meaning of a relationship, with names for its forward and reverse directions. Allowed pairs decide which record types it may connect. |
| Hierarchies | Which types may stand at the top level or under another type, connected by a containment relation. |
| Views and record pages | How records appear: tables, trees, mapping grids, relation matrices and the panels on a record page. |

The same type can be listed in several applications. It keeps the same field and relationship
rules wherever it appears. An attribute type can also be shared: changing its definition affects
every type that attaches it, while **Required** and **Read-only** belong to each attachment.

Every application can use the same kinds of view. Its name or subject does not determine its
features; the declared structure determines which views fit. The applications shipped in the
starter model are examples you may replace, reshape or remove.

## Draft, release, activation

These are three separate stages:

1. A **draft** is saved, editable work. You can leave it unfinished, close it and return later.
   Its version increases as you edit it; that number is not a release version.
2. **Installing** makes an immutable release: a fixed set of definitions with a release version.
   Later draft edits never rewrite that release.
3. **Activating** selects the installed release for one workspace. refiroo checks that workspace's
   data before switching. Other workspaces keep the releases they already run.

The editor combines the last two stages in **Install and activate…**, with a confirmation that
names the target workspace. An installed release may remain inactive if activation fails.
See [Releases](/docs/model/releases/) for compatibility and open change sets.

## Find a model and its workspaces

Open **Settings**, then **Model**. Search by model name. The list separates the model run by the
default workspace, other models in use and drafts without an installed model. It shows release
counts, the latest release, drafts and schema. The schema identifies the model language refiroo
reads; it is separate from the release version you choose for your model.

![Model list with releases, latest versions, draft counts and workspace use](/docs/screens/model-list.png)

*Above: Public transport stops of Graubünden runs the default workspace. RDM Starter Model runs
another workspace; a further draft has no installed model yet.*

Open a model for **Overview**, **Releases**, **Drafts** and **Structure**. Overview identifies the
workspaces using it; Structure initially shows the newest release read only, with a picker for other releases. Use a draft to change it.

![Model overview showing its newest release and the workspace running it](/docs/screens/model-overview.png)

*Above: the Graubünden model's overview names its running workspace and offers Change model….*

**Settings**, **Workspaces** shows the model and release beside each workspace. Open a workspace
and choose **Edit model** to work in its context. The editor says **Applies to** that workspace
and offers **Apply to this workspace…**. Check that name before applying.

![Workspaces listed with the model and release each runs](/docs/screens/model-workspaces-list.png)

*Above: Graubünden and Default run different models. Default is a workspace name here; the green
Default mark identifies Graubünden as the default workspace.*

## Who may do what

The supplied **Model administrator** role brings together model authoring and release permissions.
Administrators can also grant these separately, so the permissions and their scope matter more
than a role's name.

| Permission | What it allows |
| --- | --- |
| Model authoring | Create and edit drafts, use their editor, issues and history, and read releases. |
| Install a model | Install a draft as a release without choosing it for a workspace. |
| Model release | Install and activate releases, and migrate the workspace where the permission is granted. |
| Workspace administration | Create and manage workspaces, including creating a new target workspace. |

Authoring a draft does not itself grant permission to activate it. A workspace's **Edit model**
route needs authoring and release access there. Record editing and change-set publication need
their own data permissions. If a control is missing or unavailable, ask an access administrator
to check your grants and whether model administration is enabled on the instance.

Continue with [The model editor](/docs/model/the-model-editor/) or
[Workbook onboarding](/docs/model/workbook-onboarding/) if your starting point is a spreadsheet.

The model list orders the default workspace's model first, then other models in use, then the
rest and **Drafts without an installed model**. Pills identify **Runs the default workspace**,
**Retired** and **Draft**. A model with every release retired and no running workspace appears
under **Retired**. Open **Change model…** on Overview beside a workspace to choose its release
and check that workspace's stored data before any switch.

On **Structure**, choose **Release** to inspect that release's attributes and rules and its
relationships, other types and reverse names. This tab is read-only. Open the release to compare
or export it; open a draft to edit.

If **Model mutations are disabled** appears, installed releases remain available for inspection
and export. Ask the operator about the deployment setting before expecting draft or activation
actions. [Managing workspaces](/docs/model/managing-workspaces/) covers workspace administration.

## Continue by task

Use [Create a model draft](/docs/guide/model/create-a-model-draft/) or
[Start from a workbook](/docs/guide/model/start-a-draft-from-a-workbook/), then the
[model editor](/docs/model/the-model-editor/). [Consumer APIs](/docs/model/consumer-apis/) shapes
what consuming systems read. [Migrations](/docs/model/migrations/) covers conversions and reviewed
loss; [Model mappings](/docs/model/model-mappings/) covers data between two workspaces.

The model's name, applications and record layouts come from its definitions. The top bar uses
the default workspace model's product name; a job describes types from its own workspace's model.
A different workspace can therefore show different applications without being a different edition
of refiroo. Model drafts and activation history identify the author of changes.

A draft accepts at most 500 operations in one grouped save. Ordinary visual actions group their
related operations for you. A specialist exceeding that bound must split the work into smaller
reviewable saves, rather than repeating the refused oversized save.

When a draft is no longer needed, follow [Delete a draft](/docs/guide/model/delete-a-draft/).
Export any design you need to keep first; deleting a draft removes its saved editing work and attached workbook.

## Keep and reuse a model elsewhere

[Export an installed release](/docs/guide/model/export-a-release/) to keep its exact definitions.
On another instance, a specialist can use **New draft**, **Import JSON** to import that document,
then validate, install and choose a workspace separately. The destination must support its
model language. Importing definitions does not bring records, grants, subscriptions, workbook
files or editing history with them. For recovery of a whole installation, use the operator’s
[backup and restore procedure](/docs/run/backup-and-restore/).

guide/src/content/docs/model/record-page:
---
title: Record pages and tables
description: How a type gets its record page, and how panels and table columns show related records.
reader: model-admin
---

A record page brings one record's fields, place in a hierarchy and related records together.
A table compares records in rows. As a model administrator, you choose their arrangement in
a draft before activating it for a workspace. You need **Model authoring** to edit the layout.

A type shared by several applications can have a different page in each one. Each application
can declare one record page for that type and can offer table views with different columns.
These are model choices available to every application.

## The page a type gets

refiroo uses one rule for a new type's page, **Declare its page**, and the page shown when an
application has no declared page for the type. Adding a newly allowed relationship uses the
same rule to build its panel. The starting layout therefore does not depend on how the page
was created.

| Region | Starting content |
| --- | --- |
| **Side** | **Details**, with the type's fields in their defined order. **Hierarchy** follows when the type can have a parent. |
| **Main** | One panel for contained types, if there are any, followed by a separate panel for each relationship in each direction the type can read. |

The contained-record panel takes the first contained type's plural name as its title when
several types are listed. Relationship panels follow the model's relationship order. Their
titles read from the open record's side: the forward name for relationships it holds outwards,
the reverse name for relationships pointing towards it. A relationship with no reverse
direction is shown only from its forward side. Containment does not get another
relationship panel; its context is already shown by the hierarchy and contained records.

Each generated relationship panel starts with these columns, in this order:

- **Name** of the related record.
- A containing type's name, if all related types have the same single direct parent type.
  This column shows each related record's parent name. A hierarchy within the same type
  does not add this column.
- Up to four fields of the related types, in their defined order, without repeated fields.
- **Type**, when the panel lists more than one type.

The relationship label is omitted because the panel's title already says it. When the panel
lists one related type and has a parent column, that column is its initial sort. Otherwise,
the initial order is by name. The four-field starting limit is not a limit on the columns you
can select afterwards.

![Stop record page with separate panels for its relationships](/docs/screens/model-stop-page-relationship-panels.png)

Above: a Stop page in the guide's Graubünden model. **Details** and **Hierarchy** are at the
side. **Main** has **Served by mode**, **Operated by**, **Is represented by system code** and
**Has name translation**. System codes have a **System** column and translations a **Language**
column. These are relationships and parent types declared by this model.

## Declared pages and later changes

Without a declared page, refiroo draws the starting layout from the type's current fields,
containment and relationships. **Declare its page** saves that layout in the draft so you
can arrange it. It does not replace a page already declared.

Existing pages keep their arrangement. Adding a newly allowed relationship adds its panel
on the declared pages at both ends, where that direction is readable and no panel already
lists it. It also adds a relationship column and filter to the types' declared tables.
Removing that allowed relationship, or undoing its addition, removes the dependent layout
items that no longer have an available relationship. A panel covering other relationships
can remain with those relationships.

This does not rebuild older pages to match a new starting layout. Use **Add panel…** to
add a missing relationship panel to an existing page. It offers **Related records**,
**Contained records** where this application lists eligible contained types, and **Fields**.
The title follows the related or contained choice until you change it. Choose **Main** or
**Side** for its region. A relationship already listed is marked **(on the page)** and may
be used again. The server builds related-record and contained-record panels consistently
for every client. Applying the dialog is one draft step, with **Undo**.

Follow [Edit a record page](/docs/guide/model/edit-a-record-page/) for adding panels, moving
fields and choosing columns.

## What panels can show

| Panel | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Fields | Selected fields of the open record. Separate field groups give them different headings. |
| Contained records | One or more types that the open record can contain. |
| Related records | Records reached through selected relationships, in the outward, inward or both directions. |
| Table | Records of a type listed in the application, optionally limited to direct children of the open record. |
| Hierarchy | The parent, ancestors, or both. |

**Add panel…** creates related-record panels, contained-record panels or field groups; it
is not a form for every panel kind and setting. A specialist author maintains settings
that have no visual form. See [Applications and views](/docs/model/applications-and-views/).

Panels have a title, region, order and visibility. Ordering is separate within **Main** and
**Side**. Hiding a panel keeps its definition; removing it takes it off the page. Neither
deletes records or values. Grouping fields moves them from their current groups. **Add fields…**
adds fields omitted from the page, not new field definitions. Menus provide keyboard alternatives
to dragging panels and fields.

A list panel's **Columns…** offers the listed records' name and fields. Under **Where it sits**,
a column for a containing type shows that ancestor record's name, including ancestors beyond
the direct parent. **Type** is offered when several types are listed. These choices do not
include fields of the ancestors themselves; those are available as related-field columns
in a table view.

Related-record panels can sort by their supported column headers. Their **Sort…** layout
menu appears when the panel declares allowed sort fields. These can include name, type,
relationship, non-JSON fields of related records, and a containing type when the panel reaches
one related type. Records missing the chosen field sort last. Live timestamps are not
related-record panel sort choices. A declared initial order can be descending.

List panels can read 1–100 rows per page. A reading size limits a page of results, not the
whole collection. The record header normally shows the name and type; a declared title or
subtitle field can supply other context. The line above the title holds the list link, when
opened from a list, and the ancestors the model shows; it has no application entry. In **Record
page**, choose **Header and breadcrumbs…** to set the title, optional line under it, type label
and whether ancestors appear. Either type-name choice places the type in the header. This page-specific header does not change
the type’s shared Display attribute.

## Table columns, filters and sort

The **Table** layout tab arranges an existing table view. Columns, available filters and
initial sort are defaults for everyone using that view, rather than one person's saved search.
The view needs at least one column, filter field and sort field, with no repeats within each
list. Its initial sort must be one of its allowed sort fields. Ordinary non-JSON field columns
can sort from their headers; additional allowed fields supply further sort choices.

A relationship column shows related record names as chips in name order, with **+N more**
when they do not fit. It combines the allowed related types for that relationship at the
listed record's end. There is no fixed number of relationship columns. People can hide
columns through **Display**; a hidden relationship column is no longer read for the table.
A names column can sort only when it represents one allowed type pair and each row can have
at most one related record through it.

In **Columns…**, **Fields of** beneath a relationship unfolds the related records' fields.
**Where they sit ·** headings offer the names and fields of their containing types. Each
checked field is a column of its own; selecting it does not require selecting the relationship's
names column. Its heading combines the relationship and field labels. Each related record
contributes its value, with **—** for a missing value. A field holding JSON is not offered.
These related-field columns never sort.

For example, in the guide's Graubünden model, the Stops table can show
**Has name translation · Language code**. The value comes from the language containing each
translation, rather than from the Stop or the relationship itself.

**Filters…** offers the relationship itself, without unfolding its fields. A relationship
filter can find records linked to any selected records, linked to any record, or linked to
none. Choosing a related-field column does not provide a filter on that field. Ordinary field
filters require a filterable, non-JSON field. Fields stored on a relationship itself cannot
be columns.

Relationship columns can be declared in table views and contained-record or table panels;
they do not add columns to trees, mapping grids, relation matrices, related-record panels
or headers. The table view's **Columns…** offers the related fields directly. A panel's
**Columns…** offers its listed records' fields and **Where it sits** instead.

Follow [Choose table columns, filters and sort](/docs/guide/model/choose-table-columns-filters-and-sort/).
**The draft declares no table view** means there is no table to arrange here. Add one through
the application’s **Add a view…**; see [Add a view](/docs/guide/model/add-a-view/).

## Mark inactive records in a table

In the **Table** layout, **Inactive records…** sits beside **Filters…** and
**Sort menu and page size…**. It lets this view use one of its record type's Yes/No fields
to mark records whose value is **No**. The choice **A record is inactive when this is No**
offers **None** and the type's Yes/No fields. **None** leaves the table without an inactive
mark or switch. A field of another type, or one that is not Yes/No, is invalid for this
setting; the editor offers only eligible fields.

With a field selected, a record with **No** keeps its row and order. Its name is quieter,
with a grey **Inactive** pill when the field is called Active, or **Not** followed by the
field's name in lower case for another name. A missing value is not marked. The setting
neither changes stored values nor grants editing rights; a read-only field may be used.
It applies to this table view, rather than every table or panel listing the type.

Readers see inactive records by default and can use **Hide inactive (N)** beside **Filter**.
The switch hides exactly the marked records through a filter pill, such as **Active: not No**,
that stays in the page address. Records with no value stay visible. It works even when the
chosen field is not offered in **Filters…**. Its count is the number with **No** after the
list's search and other filters, including **0** when none match. Choosing **Yes** in the
ordinary **＋ Filter** menu instead excludes records with no value; the switch does not use
that condition. The mark and switch use the values of the current Live, change-set or
publication context; publication data remains read-only.

Follow [Choose table columns, filters and sort](/docs/guide/model/choose-table-columns-filters-and-sort/#choose-how-the-table-marks-inactive-records)
to set the field. See [Lists, search and filters](/docs/use/lists-and-filters/#show-or-hide-inactive-records)
for the reader's controls.

## Preview and validation

**Preview** draws draft definitions over live records from a chosen workspace, without changing
those records. Data-changing controls are disabled. Choose **Workspace** and **Record**, or
**Show an empty record** for a type with no records yet. Follow
[Preview a type](/docs/guide/model/preview-a-type/).

![Draft preview showing workspace and record choices](/docs/screens/model-type-preview.png)

An invalid draft cannot be previewed or laid out. **Show issues** names the definitions to
repair. Validation checks distinct panels, available fields and relationships, containment,
application membership and reading sizes. Hiding an invalid panel does not repair its
references. This model check does not prove compatibility with every stored record.

Every saved layout change is a draft history step. A refused action shows **Not applied**
and changes nothing. Review populated and empty records, check **Issues**, then follow
[Install and activate a release](/docs/guide/model/install-and-activate-a-release/).

## Panel settings and reading sizes

Open a panel’s **Settings…** in the record-page layout. The choices depend on its kind:

| Panel | Settings you can change |
| --- | --- |
| Related records | **Relationships listed**, **Listed from**, the relationship label column and allowed sort fields. Leaving the sort choices empty lists by name. |
| Hierarchy | **Show the parent** and **Show the records above the parent**, independently. |
| Contained records | **Rows on a page**. The contained types were selected when the panel was added. |
| Table | **List only the records under this one** and **Rows on a page**. The table’s record type itself needs a specialist to change. |
| Fields | No additional Settings dialog; use the field and group controls. |

**Listed from** can read **This record to the others**, **The others to this record**, or
**Both ways**. Changing direction changes which connections appear, without reversing any
stored relationship. **Show which relationship joins each record** is useful when combining
several relationships in one panel. Changing panel contents can make existing columns invalid;
check Issues and revise the columns as needed.

In **Table**, **Sort menu and page size…** chooses the fields people can sort by and the
number of **Rows on a page**. The form offers Name, current choices and fields marked Sortable.
If you remove the initial sort field, the first remaining field becomes the default. Leaving
all choices unchecked keeps the current table sort list. This differs from a related-record
panel, where no sort choices returns to name order.

Reading sizes in these forms are 10, 20, 25, 50 or 100; an existing different valid size is
also preserved as an option. The model permits 1–100. Table and contained-record panels default to 20 when no size is specified; generated table
views start at 50. A reading size does not cap a collection: people continue scrolling to read more.
Some supported declarations still need the [JSON view](/docs/model/json-view/): changing the
record type of a table panel, changing a contained panel’s type list after creation.

guide/src/content/docs/model/model-langu:
---
title: Model language versions
description: Understand unsupported model definitions and when to ask an operator for help.
reader: model-admin
---

A model language version says which definition format refiroo can read. It is separate from
the model's release version, the draft's editing version and each consumer API's contract version.
The current supported model language is **0.10**. The release and workspace screens show it as
**schema**. See [Releases](/docs/model/releases/) for selecting usable releases.

New drafts, including imported documents, accept only the current model language. The
recovery flow below applies to older releases already stored before an engine upgrade;
it is not a way to import an old document as a new draft.

Installation, activation and workspace creation refuse releases outside the supported window.
A historical release can still have readable metadata and an export even when semantic comparison
is unavailable. A workspace whose language cannot be served reports **Cannot be opened**;
this does not mean its records have been deleted.

Use the browser repair below where offered, or ask the operator to inspect the reported model
language and the version of refiroo running the instance. Older stored definitions have an offline procedure that first reports whether they
can be raised to the supported language. It leaves definitions that cannot be converted validly
or would duplicate another release and reports them. This is a deployment operation, not the
browser's **Raise contract version** action. See
[Model releases and rollback](/docs/run/model-releases-and-rollback/) for the operator's procedure.

A definition from a newer language needs a refiroo version that supports it. Changing its displayed
version or editing the language number alone does not convert it. If no workspace can be served,
or the configured startup model is outside the window, the operator must recover the deployment
before browser work can continue. Ordinary data [migrations](/docs/model/migrations/) and updating
the model document's language solve different problems.

## Reopen an older-language workspace in the browser

Where conversion is available, **Bring it up to date** offers **Review the change…** to someone
with instance-level model installation permission. Follow
[Raise a model language version](/docs/guide/model/raise-a-model-language-version/) to preview
and **Raise and reopen**. It lists every workspace using the release and leaves records, history,
change sets and publications unchanged. This recovery is a special in-place definition update;
ordinary model editing continues to create immutable releases. If the browser cannot offer the
repair, use the operator path above.

guide/src/content/docs/model/consumer-ap:
---
title: Consumer APIs in the model
description: Define the types, fields and read operations that other systems can consume.
reader: model-admin
---

A consumer API gives other systems a deliberate view of workspace data. Its contract chooses
which types and fields they read and the operations available to them. It is not a second copy
of the records. You need **Model authoring** to edit the draft; activation needs release access.
Start with [Define a consumer API](/docs/guide/model/define-a-consumer-api/).

## Choose the content within a shared form

Every consumer API uses the same patterns for presenting business objects, reading lists,
looking up values, resolving several inputs and reporting changes. Within your API, all exposed
record types share one declared object shape. Selected fields, related records, system codes,
translations and parent information fit into that shape. A field without a value uses its declared
fallback or stays empty; it does not require a different form for that record type.

Your choices supply the content: which types are exposed, what fields mean, which relationships
are followed, how lookups match and which changes are reported. The engine supplies the common
forms for objects, pages, errors and events. Systems that read your API can reuse their reading
and change-handling processes across types and contracts.

You still choose public field names, related fields and whether a relationship returns one record
or several. You also choose which operations are offered. These choices define your particular
contract; another consumer API can make different choices. A consuming system that reads the
contract's declared structure can adopt new types through configuration, while one written for
fixed names may need changes. Review the generated documents with that system's team.

Keep the agreed output stable as the underlying model evolves. The consumer contract's version
is separate from the model release version; a breaking change needs a higher contract version.
See [the shared patterns and two example record types](/docs/integrate/consumer-apis/#learn-one-way-to-read-business-objects)
for the integrator's explanation.

## From an editor choice to a consumer's answer

A **business object** is one record presented in the shape you choose for other systems.
It can include fields from that record, its parent and related records. Get by ID, lists
and lookups all return this same shape. A lookup adds a match score; a list wraps objects
in a page. Changing the shape therefore affects more than one operation.

**Reference-data example:** Stops API exposes stops, municipalities, operators and modes. A stop’s business object includes its name, stop number, operator, modes and selected system codes. An operator uses the same declared fields, with stop-specific values empty. These are choices in this model, not built-in transport features.

## The business object consumers read

On **Fields**, **Role** says which field supplies the identity, code, name or validity dates.
The identity role always reads the record's stable ID. A business code such as a stop number
is a separate field; it does not replace that ID. **Output name** controls the name in the
answer, while **Served type** shows the value's type and whether it can be missing.

![Stops API fields with output names, roles, ordered sources, served types and defaults](/docs/screens/model-consumer-tab-fields.png)

Above: Stops API in the reference model. The code has three ordered sources; stopNumber is
an integer and validTo can be null.

**Reference-data example:** Chur’s stop is named Chur, has stop number 8509000 and abbreviation CH. Its operator is Schweizerische Bundesbahnen SBB and its mode is Train. The containment path names Graubünden, Plessur and Chur, excluding the stop itself.

A field does not inherit a parent’s or related record’s value automatically. Choose the parent’s fields in **Parent**, or publish related values through an explicit related block. A single-valued relationship gives one related object or an empty value; a many-valued relationship gives a list, which can be empty. This shape follows the relationship’s cardinality and is part of the contract. Decimal values retain precision; integers, booleans and dates keep their declared types.

### The parent can carry its own values

Serve the parent when consumers need the containing record's identity and values in the same
answer as the child. On **Fields**, choose **Parent, path and hierarchy…** and turn on
**Serve the parent (objectType, id, code, name)**. Below the object's fields, **Parent** then shows **Output name** and
**Fields**. The field picker offers the built-in type, identity, code and name choices, plus
attributes attached to the types that can directly contain an exposed type. Those parent types
do not have to be exposed as business objects themselves.

Each parent field has a public output name you choose and a source it reads. In
**Parent fields…**, review the rows pairing a name with its source. The editor proposes
camelCase words for the name; you can change it. The Parent table shows name=source when
they differ. For example, a category's approval flag can be published as isApproved.

A parent field keeps its declared type. Without a default, it answers null if this parent's
type does not bind its source or the record has no value. With no parent, the whole parent
output is null. An unexposed parent's public type is null. A specialist can also give a field
ordered sources and a default, as for the object's fields. Sources must share a value type.

An existing short list of parent sources remains valid. Built-in fields keep their role's
public output name; other sources use their words in camelCase. For example, a category-code
source is served as categoryCode. Editing the parent writes out the explicit names.

Under **Parent's related records**, use **Add related**, then choose **Output name**, **Via**
and **Fields**. The relationship starts from the parent, rather than the child. The block
appears beside the parent's selected fields, as an object or list according to cardinality.
There is one parent level: it has no nested parent, path or hierarchy. The main object's path
and hierarchy remain available for ancestor names. A specialist can also select a value from
the parent's own ancestors; the field picker does not offer new ancestor sources.

**Example:** a catalogue item can carry its category's identity, an approval flag and related
external codes. The consuming system can read them together without fetching the category
separately. On a list, the category's block repeats on every child row. Consider serving a
large or rarely used block only on request.

### Serve related records always or on request

In **Types and related**, each related block has a **Served** column. The same column appears
under **Parent's related records** on **Fields**. Choose **Always** for a block in every answer,
or **On request** when consumers should explicitly ask for it. Always is the default for an
existing block and for a new one.

An on-request block is absent from an ordinary answer. When requested, it has its usual object
or list shape, including null or an empty list when there is no related record. This keeps the
default answer small without losing its declared types. On **Operations**, **Include** lists
the accepted choices automatically; edit **Served** to change that list. Parent choices have
a parent prefix there, even when you choose a different output name for the parent itself.

A filter can still use an on-request block without returning it. On **Filters**, **On related**
offers both the object's blocks and the parent's. **Keep only matching records** removes a
child if its parent's selected block has no matching item. Without that option, the filter
only trims the block. **Crosswalk** applies to the object's own blocks, not the parent's.
The filter's Name belongs to the contract; the Include parameter's name is reserved.

Turning an always-served block into an on-request block removes it from existing consumers'
ordinary answers. Review the compatibility warning and raise the contract version. Adding
parent fields or blocks, or adding filters, does not by itself require a higher version.

![Consumer API Fields tab showing Parent fields and a related block served on request](/docs/screens/model-consumer-parent-fields.png)

The Parent section shows the selected parent attributes and **Parent's related records**,
including **Via**, **Fields** and **Served**.

### Sources and defaults

Sources are tried in the displayed order, skipping missing values and empty text. Zero and
false are values, not missing data. If none supplies a value, the declared **Default** is
used; without one, the answer contains null. A default affects the output only and never
writes a value into a record. It must have the field's served type.

**Reference-data example:** the reference API has no field defaults. If you set a default abbreviation of “—”, records without an abbreviation receive that fallback in the consumer answer. Chur still shows CH. Neither record’s stored abbreviation changes.

### Values belonging to a relationship

A related block can publish values of the connection as well as values of the related record.
In its **Fields** picker, **Attributes of the relationship** lists the shared attributes carried
by the allowed pair in the selected direction. Choose a public output name for each one.
The answer uses its declared type: Yes or no stays boolean, for example. A connection without
a held value returns null for that field. If no related record exists, the whole block still
uses its usual empty object-or-list form.

These choices belong inside the related block, not the main object's **Fields**. The main object
has no single connection from which to read such a value. If a carried field is missing from
the picker, review **Via**, the exposed types and the allowed pair's **Carries** before editing
the contract. The same values appear in object reads, lists, lookups and resolved objects.
Publications retain their saved values; a business date filters validity rather than rewinding
later edits. See the [integrator's reference example](/docs/integrate/consumer-apis/#publish-values-of-the-connection)
for the resulting contract and answers.

![Consumer related-field picker showing Attributes of the relationship beside record sources](/docs/screens/model-consumer-relationship-field-picker.png)

*Above: Stops API’s Add related dialog in a reference-model draft. The proposed output
operatorLinks follows Operated by (forward) from Stop to Operator and has fields name,
localName and isPrimary. The isPrimary source list is open: Attributes of the relationship
offers Local name (text), Primary contact (boolean) and Inspected on (date), with Primary
contact selected. Built in and Attributes of the exposed types are separate groups. Nothing
has been applied.*

An **On related** filter can select one of these carried attributes in **Matches on**. It
matches that particular connection, not every object connected to the same related record.
A lookup's **Also match through** rule can also use a carried text value in **First of**.
A scored match needs text; a filter can compare other declared types, including Yes or no.
These matching choices do not require the attribute to be searchable or unique.

## Lists, filters and the requests they enable

A list selects the type to return and its order. **Within the filter** gives a list a
containment scope. A filter's **Name** becomes a parameter name; **Matches on** chooses
which values a consumer can supply. These are public choices: changing a filter name or
its accepted values can break a consuming system even if the output fields stay the same.

![Stops API filters and the records and related blocks they read](/docs/screens/model-consumer-tab-filters.png)

Above: the reference API's municipality filter matches an ancestor by ID, name or FSO
number on ordinary reads. A list's Within parameter with the same name takes parent IDs
only. Its mode filter reads related modes and keeps only matching records.

**Reference-data example:** the reference API has a list of stops within a municipality, sorted by stop number. A consumer selects the municipality by its stable identity. On a list without that special parent scope, the ordinary municipality filter can match a municipality’s name or FSO number instead. Omitting the parent selection returns the whole listed type. A page size controls one response, not the entire collection.

A related mode filter can keep only stops linked to Train and show only matching modes in their related block. Another related filter can trim the block without removing the object. A filter does not create another output field. Agree both effects with the consuming team.

## Lookups and batch answers

**XREF** finds records by the values another system knows. **Exact** and **Contains** are
numeric weights. Exact comparison ignores letter case for text; Contains matches part of
text and applies only to terms of at least three characters. A higher match score ranks
first; it is not a percentage or a guarantee that the record is the intended one.

**Reference-data example:** the stop number rule has an Exact weight of 900. Looking up 8509000 identifies Chur with that score. Looking up its Wikidata code Q663869 instead reaches Chur through a related system-code record, with the configured weight of 90. These weights rank candidates; they are not confidence percentages.

Use **Preferred types…** on an **Also match through** row to select **Prefer records of
these types**. The choices are exposed types; clear them for no preference. Review its effect
with the consuming team, especially when the same related value reaches several types.

A request for one answer succeeds only with an untied best candidate. No match and a tied best score are distinct outcomes. **Also match through** lets related records identify their owners. **First of** uses the first matching related rule; **Prefers** can choose which exposed owner types receive its score.

**Resolve** applies Get by ID or lookup rules to many inputs. Each gets its own found, missing, ambiguous or refused outcome, in input order. Shared request filters can be overridden for an individual item; those defaults narrow the question, whereas a field’s Default fills a missing output value. **Crosswalk** enables asking for a selected related representation, such as a system code. It does not resolve a tied source match by guessing which source has a target.

## Events describe changes to the output

An event's **Types** selects the records, **Changes** selects creation, update or deletion,
and **Watches** limits which output changes trigger an update event. Leaving Watches empty
watches any change to the business object, including related blocks. **Events per type**
adds a standard event for each exposed type. The reference API leaves that option off
and declares only its custom `stops-changed` event.

**Reference-data example:** Stops API watches code, name and validity dates. Renaming Chur to Chur Bahnhof produces an update notification naming the name output. Changing latitude alone does not trigger that event. This is an example change, not a record of a change in the reference snapshot.

A related record’s edit or a relationship joining or leaving a watched block can also trigger an update.
Changes to a parent's selected attributes, values read from its ancestors or items in its
related blocks can report an update for each child showing that parent. Watch the parent
output, or leave Watches empty, to cover those changes. Events and webhook deliveries have
no Include choice: their full objects leave on-request blocks out.
If a block exposes connection values, an update of that relationship can report the block as
changed too. Add the block to **Watches**, or leave Watches empty to include all output changes.
A notification watching only unrelated main fields does not report that edit. Watched source changes can be reported even if a fallback leaves the displayed answer equal. A validity date passing without a write produces no notification. Moving a record into an event’s types counts as creation, moving it out as deletion, and moving between included types as an update to its type.

Full notifications carry current business objects when delivered, rather than a saved historical copy. Deleted records have no object body. Declaring an event does not register a receiver or grant access. Administrators manage delivery separately; see [Webhooks](/docs/administer/webhooks/).

## What the editor shows

Select **Consumer APIs** in the model pane, then an API. Its facts show **Contract version** and
**Compatible with what consumers read**, **Needs contract version …**, or **Checked once the
draft is valid**. Fix model errors before relying on the compatibility result.

| Tab | What you decide or inspect |
| --- | --- |
| Types and related | Exposed record types, their public names, related blocks and optional parent, path and hierarchy. |
| Fields | Output names, value sources and roles. Ordered sources use the first non-empty value. |
| Operations | Get by ID, cross-reference and resolve choices, lists and custom events. |
| Filters | Named ways to narrow or match records, including through related blocks. |
| Schema | The generated description of the data shape. |
| Message example | A generated example of the declared shape, rather than a live record sample. |

![Consumer API definition on the Types and related tab](/docs/screens/model-consumer-tab-types.png)

A field's **Output name** is the word consumers receive. **Sources…** chooses the fields it
reads, in order; **Role** identifies a purpose used by the contract. **Add related…** follows
an allowed relationship and selects the related fields to expose. The declaration can also
serve parent, path and hierarchy information.

## Operations and matching

**Get by ID**, **XREF** and **Resolve** are offered for the API’s exposed types. **Resolve**
requires both Get by ID and XREF; **Events per type** enables the standard type events. Lists specify **Of**,
an optional **Within the filter** and **Sorted by**. Cross-reference rules choose how values
identify related records. Matching can use **Exact** and **Contains** weights and **Also match
through** a related block. Check **Matches on…**, **Fields…**, **First of** and **Prefers** where
shown rather than assuming the display name is the unique identifier.

Filters have a **Name** and **Verb**: **By type**, **Under**, **Linked to** or **On related**.
Their further choices depend on what they read. **Through** can use the record itself, a related
block or records sharing that block. **On related** can keep only matching records, score only
matching items or expose a crosswalk. These choices change what a consumer can ask and receive.
Custom events select **Types**, **Changes** and **Watches**; leaving Watches empty watches any
change to what consumers read. An event declaration does not create a delivery subscription.

## Contracts, access and limits

A contract version is separate from the model release version, draft version and model language
version. Removing or changing something consumers read can require a higher contract version.
Renaming a public field or changing relationship cardinality can affect the output too. Review
the differences with the consuming teams, then
[raise the contract version](/docs/guide/model/raise-a-contract-version/). Raising it keeps the previous definition served beside the new version by default. The editor preserves the definition from the draft’s base release, including when the draft already contains breaking edits. An API or version not served by that base release has no previous definition to retain. An invalid model still needs repair.

A consuming system needs a client granted this particular API in each workspace it reads.
Defining the API, granting a role or giving a person Model authoring does not grant consumer
access. A security administrator manages these grants. Without the API grant, a data read
is refused with Forbidden; the consumer does not receive a reduced version of the object.
Agree the exposed fields with that administrator: a grant opens this API's declared output,
not a field-by-field selection.
**Rename…** changes its display name; **Describe…** supplies its generated description.
A released key identifies consumers' existing access point: keep it stable. A released API's
key can still be changed, but consumers of the old key then get 404, as with removal. Removing an API
stops its consumers reading it once active. Review that warning even where removal is allowed.

A specialist can edit the definition or an item as one saved step.
No visual form covers every detail of the model language. Use the
[specialist view](/docs/model/json-view/) with a specialist for unsupported combinations, then inspect
Issues and the generated documents. Do not infer support solely from a field being accepted as text.

See [the generated documents](/docs/guide/model/see-a-consumer-apis-documents/) for review and handover;
integrators use [Integrate](/docs/integrate/overview/) for requests and authentication.

## Review edits that remove behavior

Turning **XREF** off asks **Stop offering XREF?**. It removes the match rules and also stops
**Resolve**, which depends on XREF. **Undo** restores the step; switching XREF on again starts
without those rules. Inspect the contract changes before activating. An operation not declared
in the contract is unavailable to consumers and absent from its generated operation document.

A field's editable **Default** supplies its declared fallback when sources do not yield a value;
it differs from a default on a record attribute. An identity-role output reads the record's
stable ID; publish other identifiers as separate fields. Output roles must not conflict, related
blocks must name valid relationships, and a filter must choose one kind of read. The Issues
list points to invalid references or combinations.

The model language also supports per-type events, watched fields and related blocks, scoped
lists and parameters based on types, ancestors or related records. Use the specialist document
view for declarations the current form does not expose. Reducing event coverage, changing
crosswalk availability or removing an operation can require a higher contract version just as
removing a field does. Adding more output is usually compatible; lowering a contract version
is refused.

*Source for the reference examples: opentransportdata.swiss, Service Points (Didok), Federal Office of Transport / SBB, snapshot 2026-11-02. Wikidata, CC0.*

## Keep an earlier version available

Use this when consuming systems need time to move to a changed contract. In the model
editor, select the consumer API and open **Types and related**. You need **Model authoring** to edit;
the release must then be installed and activated in each workspace that serves it.

1. Raise **Contract version** when changing what existing consumers read. **Raise contract
   version to …** advances it by one. The editor keeps the definition from the draft’s base
   release, rather than copying any breaking edits already made in the draft. An API or
   version not served by that base release leaves no earlier version to keep.
2. Make the breaking edits to the new current version. In **Earlier versions**, check the
   retained **Version**, **Superseded** day and **Sunset day**. Earlier versions keep their
   output shape but read current data; they are not historical copies of records.
3. To announce an end date, select the row's **Sunset day** value or its pencil. In
   **Sunset day (YYYY-MM-DD)**, enter the calendar date and choose **Save**. Emptying it and
   saving withdraws the announcement; the table then shows a dash. A refused date stays in
   the form with **Not saved** and its reason; the saved date is unchanged. Correct it and
   save again, or **Cancel**. The day is announced to consumers in the response's Sunset
   header after activation. It is an announcement: refiroo serves the version until you
   explicitly stop it, whatever the date.
4. Review Issues and the generated documents, then install and activate the release. Installing
   alone does not change a workspace. Existing consumers and webhooks on a retained version
   continue using that version's shape.

The model administrator chooses the notice period with the consuming teams. The software's
own compatibility period does not impose a deadline on your organisation's consumer APIs.

If you already made breaking edits, **Needs contract version …** offers **Raise to version …**
and **Raise and stop serving version …**. **Raise to version …** keeps the base release’s
definition while your edited definition becomes the new version. Choosing
**Raise and stop serving version …** instead leaves no copy of the
version being replaced. Use that choice only when its consumers are ready to lose access.

![Earlier versions table with a retained version, superseded day, sunset day and Stop serving](/docs/screens/model-consumer-earlier-versions.png)

### Stop serving and undo

In **Earlier versions**, choose **Stop serving** for the intended version. Read the confirmation:
consumers lose access once the draft is active. Cancel to keep serving it, or confirm the removal.
**Undo** restores that draft step before activation. Review compatibility, install and activate
the release only after the receiving teams have moved. Stopping an earlier version preserves
records and other versions. It stops that version's reads and suspends subscriptions bound to it;
ask the integration administrator to check the receiver before resuming on the current version.

Follow [Stop serving an earlier contract version](/docs/guide/model/stop-serving-an-earlier-contract-version/) for the sunset announcement, removal and undo steps.

After activation, restoring service needs a release that retains the original definition again;
an old installed release does not keep a route running by itself. Do not recreate an earlier
version with a changed shape under the same number.

### When the retained version prevents activation

Every retained version must still refer to types, fields and relationships present in the new
model. Keep those sources while consumers need them. An issue names the version and the missing
source; restore the source or coordinate stopping that version.

A retained number must be lower than the current version and appear only once. Invalid dates,
duplicate numbers and invalid references must be corrected before release. If a kept contract
would change, the finding says **a kept version is served as it was: restore it, or stop serving
it**. Raising the current version again does not repair the retained copy. The install review
shows this finding rather than offering a version-raise fix for it. A warning that a version
stops serving is expected only when removal is deliberate; inspect it before activation.

## Edit version and remove a contract

The API’s **Settings** table has an editable **Contract version**. Enter a positive whole
number and Save, or Cancel to leave it unchanged. The menu’s **Raise contract version to …**
advances it by one without typing. Lowering a version is refused; increasing it does not
repair an invalid definition. When the draft’s base release served the version being raised, its definition appears in **Earlier versions** and remains available after activation.

Use **Remove consumer API** only after coordinating with its consumers. The confirmation
warns that they receive 404 once this draft is active. Cancel keeps it; Undo restores a saved
removal in the draft. Existing releases remain immutable, but do not keep the old contract
running in a workspace that activates the new model.

**Edit as JSON…** on the API edits its complete definition as one step; on a row, it edits
that item. These are specialist controls, not a prerequisite for the named forms. Ask a
specialist to handle combinations the forms do not expose, then review Issues, compatibility
and the generated documents again.

---
title: How workbook proposals are made
description: Understand the patterns behind proposed types, lists, keys and relationships, and check their limits.
reader: model-admin
---

With **Model authoring**, use the evidence behind a workbook proposal to decide whether it describes
your data correctly. The rules look at column values, repetition, headings and shared identifiers. They do not know
what a stop, municipality or operator means. Choosing to propose from a workbook applies the
suggestions as draft steps; it does not install a model or load records.

Select a **Proposed** element, read **Proposed because**, then open **Evidence**. Use
[Map a column](/docs/guide/model/map-a-column/) to change its interpretation, or
[Propose again](/docs/guide/model/propose-again-with-a-newer-workbook/) to reconsider the file.
Your manual edits are retained. The percentages below are recognition rules, not confidence
scores, and cannot be tuned in the mapping form.

## Keys and names

The first suitable fully filled, distinct column is proposed as the key. Text without spaces
and whole numbers take precedence over a GUID. A GUID is the fallback when every row has a
different one. The proposed name is another text column filled on at least 95% of rows, excluding
code-like columns and lookups; a heading containing “name” takes precedence. If a text key would
leave no name beside a GUID, the GUID becomes the key and the text becomes the name.

Check that the proposed key stays stable between files. A different value on every row is not
proof that a column identifies the same real record next month.

## Lists, parents and connections

| Shape in the workbook | What refiroo proposes and what to check |
| --- | --- |
| A code and its name | A list with code and name, or the row's own identifying fields. The rule allows at most 1.5 names per code on average and expects each name to belong to one code in at least 98% of groups. |
| Different names for one code | A value map from less frequent names to the most frequent one. Check the correct spelling before accepting a majority choice. |
| A repeated text column | A parent when there are at most a third as many distinct values as rows and other columns stay constant in at least 98% of its groups. A constant code or GUID can identify the parent. |
| More than one repeated parent candidate | The first becomes the parent; further ones become related lists. A record has one parent. Empty parent cells allow records at the top level. |
| Numbered level headings, or references to the same sheet's keys | A hierarchy. A parent-code column needs at least 90% of its values to match the sheet's keys; empty parent codes identify roots. |
| A few repeated text values | A lookup list when there are at most 50 distinct values and no more than 20% as many values as filled cells. An ordinary text field remains an alternative. |
| Values matching another sheet | A relationship when at least 90% of distinct values match the other sheet's keys or names. One referenced record per row can still be shared by many rows. |
| Several values in one cell | A many-valued relationship when a delimiter occurs in at least 10% of cells and at least 80% of its parts also occur as whole values. Check the delimiter before splitting. |
| Several Yes/No columns | One relationship to a list whose members come from the headings. Recognised sets are Y/N, yes/no, X/empty, true/false and 1/0. The columns need not be adjacent. A nearby multi-valued column can join the set. A lone Yes/No column becomes a field with a value map. |
| A GUID column left over | An external identifier. Check which related record and system it describes rather than relying on its shape alone. |

Text averaging more than 60 characters is treated as description text, not a parent, lookup or
code's name. Remaining columns become typed attributes; a candidate key can make one unique.
Placeholder suggestions map values such as N/A, ?, TBC and a dash to empty. Read the affected
counts: an intentional value must not disappear because it resembles a placeholder.

Matching headers and value types across sheets can share an attribute definition. It is proposed
as unique only when the sheets do not share its values. Two or more lists proposed from a sheet
can be gathered into a navigation group. Generated labels come from headings and sheet names,
with underscores and joined capitals separated; you can rename them all. When table headings repeat,
the proposal leaves a later same-named column out and reports a warning. Review those columns
manually; the mapping and loading facilities can distinguish repeated headings by numbered names.

## Names in several languages

A sheet with no key can describe names for another sheet's records when it has at least two
ISO 639-1 language codes or English language names and at least 90% of the reference column's
distinct values match that sheet's keys, once per language. Columns such as Name (de) and Name FR
can also be recognised as language variants of a name column.

Repeated base values can reveal translated columns even without useful headings. The translation
must have 80%–125% as many distinct values as the base, at least 80% correspondence in each
direction, and at most half its rows identical to the base. A recognised language in the heading
names it; otherwise the proposal uses **Language 1**, **Language 2**, and so on. Rename these
before loading. A translation of a type's name becomes a related name record; translations of
other base fields remain attributes. Similar-looking columns alone do not establish their language.

## Sheets that describe fields

A workbook can describe a model rather than contain its records. refiroo checks this shape first,
then excludes the description and the referenced list sheets from ordinary table interpretation.
It looks for a filled, distinct text column naming fields, a column with at least 80% recognised
field-type words and a target column with at least half its cells naming other sheets. The
recognition uses values, rather than requiring particular headings. Automatic description detection
checks sheets with up to 1,000 data rows; type-word and target columns must each have at most
200 distinct values to be considered. Outside these bounds, map the file deliberately rather
than expecting this proposal.

| Field-type words | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| lookup, list, reference, select | Choose one record from the target list. |
| multi, multiple, multi-select, multi-lookup | Choose several records. |
| flag, yes/no, boolean, checkbox | A member of a target flag set; a Yes/No field without a target. |
| text, string | Text field. |
| long text, description | Long text field. |
| number, integer | Whole number field. |
| decimal | Decimal field. |
| date | Date field. |

An unrecognised word produces a text field and a warning. The described type takes the sheet's
name. Target sheets supply lists using their IDs and names. Placeholder IDs are skipped; a sheet
holding only placeholders produces a list to define, with no loaded records and a warning. A target
without a sheet produces an empty list too. Placeholder recognition here also includes “to be
defined”, “to be decided” and “to be confirmed”.

Review the resulting type and empty lists before installing. A description does not create
instances of the type it describes.

## Extend a model using another file

Files meet through the stored model and records. Install and load the first file before using
**Additions to the model** for a second file that refers to its records. Choose the comparison
workspace deliberately; without an explicit workspace the comparison uses the default workspace.

A sheet can match a type by its name, by at least 50% overlap between its keys and stored unique
values or names, or by headings matching at least half of the type's field and relationship names
(at least two). Name comparison ignores case, accents, punctuation and ordinary plural endings.
A same-named attribute is reused when at least 95% of cells fit its value type; a shared global
attribute is preferred to a new one. Existing allowed relationships are reused.

A code column matching at least half of a stored unique field's values takes precedence over name
matching. Missing IDs are reported with their rows; creating missing records is an alternative,
not an assumed repair. If an ID has a different name in the file, the stored name stands by default;
loading the new name is an alternative. Resolve drift explicitly before loading.

## Sheets laid out as lists

When a sheet has several blocks, a block with at least three columns and 60% of the sheet's
cells is treated as its main table. Other blocks are named in warnings. Without a main table,
a sheet laid out for reading can be interpreted list by list when no more than 2,000 rows hold
cells. This also covers several lists stacked in a block of at most two columns. Colour, bold
text and merged-cell formatting do not determine the structure.

Empty columns and rows separate ranges. A row above a range can be its header; a single cell
above several neighbouring lists can be their shared title. Text averaging over 60 characters
is treated as prose rather than list data. Inspect **Under**, **Cells** and **Note** to confirm
the inferred titles and boundaries. **Proposed**, **Loaded** and **Not loaded** distinguish
interpretations in the source pane; Loaded here means a source reads the list, not that its
records have already been published.

The first column supplies names and identifies list items. Within the range, a Yes/No column
becomes a field; several such columns form a flag set. A text column filled on at least 80%
of the rows with names can be proposed as translated names. A language word in its heading
names that language; otherwise you must rename the proposed language. Columns containing only
a heading are reported and not read; remaining columns become fields.

English note words such as “multiple answers”, “multiple choice”, “multi-select” or “several”
indicate several choices. “Single answer”, “single choice” and “one answer” indicate one.
“Free field” or “free text” identifies free answers rather than a list. A header with no values
or a free-answer range proposes no list and raises a warning. Recognised note rows are skipped,
and their note becomes the type's description. An extra heading row in a flag list can also be
recognised and skipped; it does not become a record.

Two or more lists beneath one innermost title can form a navigation group. At least three with
the same column kinds under one title, or none, also offer **Read these N lists as one list under
their headers**. The initial proposal keeps them separate because shape alone cannot tell
whether their headings are categories or independent lists.

Follow [Read lists in a sheet](/docs/guide/model/read-lists-in-a-sheet/) to adjust a range or
choose that alternative. Adjusting a range keeps column bindings by their column letters.
**Don't load this list** removes its source and can remove its proposed type when nothing else
loads, relates to or contains it. Review History and Issues after that choice. Always finish
with the [current dry run](/docs/guide/model/check-a-workbook-with-a-dry-run/).

---
title: Rotate a client secret
description: Make a replacement secret, switch the integration during an overlap and end the old secret.
reader: access-admin
---

You need **Security administration**. Arrange the handover with the integration owner
before a routine rotation. See [Clients](/docs/administer/clients/) for how secrets and grants differ.
Rotating the secret preserves the client ID, name and grants.

## Choose an overlap

1. Open **Settings › Connections › Clients** and select the intended client. Check its name
   and **Client ID**. Inspect **Secrets**, including the last four characters, **Valid until**
   and **Last used**, so you can distinguish the current secret from a previous one.
2. Choose **Rotate secret…**. Select how long the current secret should keep working:
   **1 hour**, **24 hours** (the default), or **7 days**. Use enough time for the agreed handover.
3. If the secret may have leaked, choose **Stop it now**. The system is refused when it
   next tries to authenticate with the old secret until it has the replacement.
4. Choose **Rotate secret**. **Cancel** leaves the secrets unchanged. If creation fails,
   read **No new secret was made**, reload the client and check its current secrets before retrying.

![Rotate secret dialog with overlap choices and Make a new secret](/docs/screens/admin-client-rotate.png)

*Above: Stops reader (guide) is set for a 24-hour overlap in the reference dialog; no rotation has been submitted.*

## Save and switch

1. Copy the new secret from **New secret for …** into the agreed secure store. The dialog
   shows it once and says when the previous secret ends. Choose **I have copied it** after saving it.
2. Have the integration owner replace the configured secret while keeping the same client ID.
   For an active client, both old and new secrets work for authentication during the overlap.
3. Ask them to prove a fresh sign-in and the intended operation with the new secret.
   Check its **Last used** time in **Secrets**; a system still using existing access may
   not have tested the replacement yet.
4. Let the overlap expire, or use **End now** for the previous secret after checking the
   new one works. Match the last four characters carefully before ending an older secret.

If the new secret was not saved before the dialog closed, it cannot be displayed again.
Make another replacement and coordinate that handover. If access is refused after the overlap,
check that every running copy of the integration has switched and that the client remains active.

A rotation applies the overlap to every older still-valid secret, keeping any earlier
expiry. Repeated rotations do not extend an old handover window. Ending a secret alone prevents new authentication; it does not end access already issued.

## Recover after a leaked secret

1. Open the client and choose **Deactivate**. Confirm the deactivation. Its requests are
   refused from their next request, including requests using access already issued. Its
   name, ID and grants remain.
2. In **Deactivated**, select the same client and choose **Rotate secret…**. The dialog
   explains that the new secret takes effect when you restore the client. Rotation does
   not restore it.
3. Choose **Stop it now**, then **Rotate secret**. This ends every older still-valid
   secret immediately. Copy the replacement from **New secret for …** and store it before
   choosing **I have copied it**. Have the integration owner configure the replacement.
4. Review the retained grants and the lifetime of access issued before deactivation with
   the integration owner. Restoring the client can allow that earlier access again if it
   has not expired; replacing a secret does not revoke it.
5. When the client is safe to use, choose **Restore**. It takes effect immediately. Have
   the integration owner prove fresh authentication with the new secret and the intended
   operation, then check **Last used**.

![Rotate secret for a deactivated client, with Stop it now selected](/docs/screens/admin-client-inactive-rotate.png)

An overlap starts when **Rotate secret** succeeds, including time spent deactivated.
It does not restart when you choose **Restore**. For example, restoring two hours after a
one-hour overlap leaves only the new secret usable. Restoring within that hour lets an
older secret authenticate until its existing deadline. Use **Stop it now** for a leaked
secret rather than leaving that window open.

---
title: Create a webhook
description: Choose a source and receiver, select events and store the signing key.
reader: access-admin
---

Use this task when another system needs to receive changes as they happen. You need **Integration administration** in the source workspace and a receiver prepared by its integration owner. Read [The Webhooks page](/docs/administer/webhooks/) for delivery rules and limits.

When **Webhooks are off in this deployment** appears, the page offers **Open Deployment**
instead of **New webhook**. Ask the operator to enable delivery before starting these steps.

![The New webhook dialog with its source, event and delivery choices](/docs/screens/admin-webhook-new.png)

## Choose what is sent

1. Open **Settings › Connections › Webhooks** and choose **New webhook**. If webhooks are off, ask the operator to enable them. Workspace events need no consumer API declaration.
2. In **Webhook**, enter a readable **Name** and the receiver’s **URL**. Use its final HTTPS address; redirects are not followed. Private and localhost receivers need the operator to allow private destinations on this instance. Plain HTTP is accepted only for a localhost receiver when the operator has allowed private destinations. Link-local destinations are always refused. If the address is refused, ask the operator to review it before trying again.
3. In **Source › Events from**, choose **Consumer API** for declared record changes, or **Workspace events** for change-set steps. If no consumer API declares events, only **Workspace events** is offered. For a consumer source, select **Consumer API** too.
4. Select **Workspace**. The list offers active workspaces where you hold Integration administration. Check the source and workspace carefully: they cannot be changed after creation.
5. Under **Events**, keep **All events**, or select **Chosen events**, then **Choose events** and the required entries. At least one event is required. For workspace events the choices are **change-set.submitted** (submitted for approval), **change-set.approved** (approved and published), and **change-set.sent-back** (returned to its author). **All events (3)** selects all three.
6. For a consumer source, under **Filters**, leave none to receive every event of the chosen kinds, or choose **Add filter**. Enter each value and press Enter. Several values for one filter are alternatives. If there are no declared filters, none can be added here. Workspace events have no **Consumer API** selector, **Filters** or **Content** choices.

![Workspace events selected in New webhook, with change-set event choices and delivery options](/docs/screens/admin-webhook-workspace-events.png)

## Agree the delivery choices

1. Under **Delivery › Requests**, keep **One event per request**, or choose **Batched** and set **Up to (events)** within the displayed limit. A batch sends available events without waiting to fill up.
2. For a consumer source, choose **Content**: **With the object** for the current record, or **Notification only** when the receiver reads details itself. Workspace events describe a change-set step instead. For either source, agree **Format** with the receiving system’s owner: **RDM JSON** or **CloudEvents 1.0**.
3. Choose **Add webhook**. A refusal appears beside the relevant field or as **The webhook was not created**. Correct the stated problem and try again. **Cancel** leaves without creating it.

## Store the key and check delivery

1. In **Keep the signing key**, copy the key directly into the receiver’s secure configuration or the agreed secret store. It is shown once. Choose **I have stored the key** only after storing it. Do not include a real key in screenshots or messages.
2. Check the webhook’s **Configuration**, including its source, destination and state. Creation starts with future changes; it does not send a copy of existing records. Arrange initial synchronisation separately with the integration owner.
3. After an intended live record change or selected change-set step, open **Deliveries** and choose **Refresh**. Open the event to read its attempts and response. **Succeeded** means the receiver accepted it; ask its owner to check the resulting data too.
4. For **Retrying** or **Suspended**, follow [Find out why a webhook paused](/docs/guide/administer/find-out-why-a-webhook-paused/). If the key was lost before being saved, use [Rotate a webhook key](/docs/guide/administer/rotate-a-webhook-key/); the original cannot be displayed again.

---
title: Require a second factor
description: Require a second step for password sign-in and check the result.
reader: access-admin
---

Use this policy when a password alone should not sign people in. You need **Security administration**.
It applies to local password sign-in, including recovery administrators, with the exception below. Provider sign-ins
use their provider's own checks. Read [Sign-in and second factors](/docs/administer/sign-in/)
for passkeys, sessions and recovery.

An account whose sign-in is managed by an administrator cannot set up its own second factor.
If it has neither an authenticator app nor a passkey, it is not asked to set one up: it signs
in with its password alone even with this requirement on. Existing factors still apply.
Review these accounts in [People and groups](/docs/administer/people-and-groups/#sign-in-managed-by-an-administrator)
before relying on the policy to require a second step for everyone.

## Prepare people

1. Tell people who manage their own sign-in that password sign-in needs an authenticator app or passkey. They can prepare
   on their own **Settings › Account** page using **Set up an authenticator app** or
   **Add a passkey**. See [Your account](/docs/use/account/).
2. Ask people using an app to save the recovery codes shown at setup somewhere they can
   reach without that device. Each code works once. Someone with another registered passkey
   has another way in if a device is lost.
3. Check that an administrator can help with lost devices. If nobody can sign in, recovery
   requires an operator on the server; turning this policy on includes the recovery administrators too.

## Turn the requirement on

1. Open **Settings › People and access › Sign-in** and select **Local accounts**.
   Under **Second factor**, find **Require a second factor with a password**.
2. Tick it. The **Require a second factor?** confirmation explains that people without a
   factor must set up an app on the sign-in page before a session starts. The administrator-managed
   accounts described above are exempt from that setup.
3. Choose **Require it** to apply the policy. **Cancel** leaves it unchanged.
   Wait for the setting to show as checked. There is no separate Save button.
4. At the next password sign-in, check that someone with a factor is asked for the second
   step. Someone who manages their own sign-in and has neither an app nor a passkey must complete setup and save the recovery
   codes before continuing. A registered passkey also meets the requirement. For a managed
   account with no factor, check that password sign-in continues without setup.

![Local accounts settings showing the second-factor requirement checkbox](/docs/screens/admin-signin-local.png)

*Above: the reference instance shows the requirement before it is enabled. No policy was changed for this capture.*

## Correct a problem or turn it off

If the change is refused, read **Not changed**, reload the settings and check the saved
state before trying again. Someone whose app codes fail should check their phone's time
and use a recovery code or another registered passkey if available. Follow
[Help someone who lost a device](/docs/guide/administer/help-someone-who-lost-a-device/)
when they have no remaining method.

To stop requiring the second step, clear **Require a second factor with a password**.
This saves immediately. It does not remove anyone's configured app or passkeys; an account
with an authenticator app continues to use it until that factor is removed.
People cannot remove their own required factor while the requirement is on.

Changing this policy does not end existing sessions. To require a particular person to
sign in again, open their People page and use **Sign out everywhere**, then check their
next password sign-in. Do not treat an already open session as a test of the new policy.

---
title: Link a provider sign-in to an existing person
description: Join a new provider identity to the person’s existing account while keeping their roles and history.
reader: access-admin
---

Use this task when someone already has an account and their first organisation-provider sign-in created another person. You need **Security administration**. refiroo never links accounts just because their e-mail addresses match. Read [People and groups](/docs/administer/people-and-groups/).

1. Confirm the person’s identity through your organisation’s process. Identify the existing account whose roles and history should continue, and the new person created by provider sign-in. Check e-mail addresses and sign-in methods as well as names.
2. Open **Settings › People and access › People** and select the new provider person. Do this before giving that new person a password, direct roles or local group memberships; those additions make linking unsafe and are refused.
